quiz.why: The common 'right action' pattern is disclose, decline, report and protect. Hiding, delaying and denying are wrong.

quiz.q: If the Code is stricter than the law:
quiz.why: If the Code is stricter than the law, follow the Code, because the stricter rule applies to you.
The US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) dates from 1977.

questions.q: Gifts during a live tender are:
questions.why: Gifts during a live tender are not allowed, whatever the amount, because they could influence the decision.

questions.q: UPSI must not be:
questions.why: UPSI must not be traded on or shared, under the SEBI PIT Regulations.

questions.q: DPDP Data Processor acts:
questions.why: A DPDP Data Processor acts on behalf of a fiduciary, not for itself.

questions.q: First step for a conflict of interest:
questions.why: The first step for a conflict of interest is to disclose it.

questions.q: Price-fixing regulator:
questions.why: The CCI is the regulator for price-fixing and other competition matters.

questions.q: Vigil mechanism law:
questions.why: The vigil mechanism comes from the Companies Act 2013 (Section 177).

questions.q: Which is a rationalisation?
questions.why: 'They owe me' is a rationalisation, a justification for wrongdoing. Audit, approval and disclosure are controls.

questions.q: Consent withdrawal must be:
questions.why: Withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it (Section 6).

questions.q: UK Bribery Act covers private bribery:
questions.why: Yes. The UK Bribery Act covers bribery of private parties as well as public officials.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A company is safe if directors did not know of an agent's bribe. Reason (R): Section 9 allows a defence of adequate procedures.
questions.why: The assertion is false, because directors' ignorance is not the defence; the reason is true: Section 9 allows a defence of adequate procedures.

questions.q: Max DPDP penalty for breach of children's obligations:
questions.why: The maximum DPDP penalty for breach of children's obligations is ₹200 crore, per the Schedule.

questions.q: Which is NOT a legitimate use under S.7?
questions.why: Targeted ads to children are not a legitimate use under Section 7; they are prohibited. Medical emergencies, court orders and employment can be legitimate uses.

questions.q: Case: Your team lead's spouse runs a vendor your team uses; nobody disclosed it. You should:
questions.why: An undisclosed conflict like a team lead's spouse running a vendor should be raised with compliance. Ignoring it or confronting the spouse is wrong.

questions.q: Case: You must pay a ₹500 'tip' to a clerk to get a certified copy that has an official fee of ₹100. Best action?
options: Pay only the official fee with receipt; decline the tip; report
questions.why: Pay only the official fee against a receipt, decline the ₹500 tip and report it. The extra payment is a facilitation payment, which is banned.

questions.q: Case: You receive a stranger's payslip by email by mistake. Best action?
options: Inform the sender/privacy team and delete it
questions.why: Receiving a stranger's payslip by mistake is a possible data breach, so inform the sender or privacy team and delete it. Posting or keeping it makes it worse.

questions.q: Case: Analyst knows of an unannounced acquisition and buys shares through his mother's account. This is:
questions.why: Buying shares on unannounced acquisition news through his mother's account is insider trading. Indirect trading is also prohibited.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: PCA 2018 – commercial organisation liability; DPDP – Board appeals to TDSAT
questions.why: PCA 2018 introduced commercial organisation liability, and DPDP Board appeals go to TDSAT. The other pairs mix up the laws and regulators.

questions.q: Case: A Significant Data Fiduciary hasn't appointed a DPO in India or done data audits. Maximum penalty category?
questions.why: A Significant Data Fiduciary that hasn't appointed a DPO in India or done data audits faces a penalty of up to ₹150 crore.

questions.q: Case: Sales VP: 'Agree on price with rival, use an agent to pay the tender officer, and send the customer list to the agent on WhatsApp.' Laws engaged?
questions.why: Agreeing prices with a rival engages the Competition Act, paying a tender officer engages the PCA, and sending a customer list on WhatsApp engages DPDP.

corp-cyber.title: Cybersecurity awareness for every employee
corp-cyber.description: Chapter-by-chapter cyber awareness: threats and the CIA triad, phishing and social engineering, passwords, MFA and passkeys, safe devices and networks, and what to do in an incident — with Indian reporting channels.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Security foundations and today's threats
courses.summary: Why attackers target ordinary employees, the CIA triad, who the attackers are, and the most common attack types — malware, ransomware, account takeover and fraud.
outcomes: Learners can explain confidentiality, integrity and availability with examples
Learners can name common threat actors and their motives
Learners can describe how malware and ransomware spread
Learners can explain why humans are the main target

scenes.text: Monday: salary data is emailed to the wrong list. Tuesday: someone changes a vendor's bank account in the ERP.
Wednesday: the billing system is down for six hours after an attack.
The CISO says each day broke a different side of the same triangle.

steps.title: Three goals of security
steps.body:
- **Confidentiality:** only authorised people can see information (salary data leak breaks it).
- **Integrity:** information is accurate and not altered without authorisation (changed bank details break it).
- **Availability:** systems and data are usable when needed (outage breaks it).

steps.title: Controls for each
steps.body:
- Confidentiality → access control, encryption, need-to-know, data classification.
- Integrity → approvals, checksums/hashes, audit logs, segregation of duties.
- Availability → backups, redundancy, patching, DDoS protection, disaster recovery.

steps.title: Solved example: classify incidents
steps.body:
**1)** Laptop with unencrypted customer data stolen → **Confidentiality**.
**2)** Attacker edits invoice amounts → **Integrity**.
**3)** Ransomware encrypts file servers → **Availability** (and often confidentiality too, when data is stolen before encryption).

steps.title: Solved example: pick a control
steps.body:
Problem: finance staff can change vendor bank accounts alone.
**Step 1:** Which side? Integrity.
**Step 2:** Control: require a second approver and call-back verification on a known number before any bank change.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking security = only confidentiality.
- Believing 'our data isn't interesting' — attackers want money, access and credentials from everyone.

activity.prompt: Which side of the triad is hit first?

items.text: Customer list posted on a forum
Fake entries added to audit logs

options: Data is accurate and not tampered with
quiz.why: Integrity means data is accurate and has not been tampered with. Secrecy is confidentiality and uptime is availability.
A DDoS attack floods a service so it becomes unavailable, so it mainly targets availability.
Encryption makes data unreadable to outsiders, so it mainly protects confidentiality.

quiz.q: Second approval for bank changes protects:
quiz.why: A second approval for bank changes prevents unauthorised changes, protecting integrity.
Backups mainly support availability, since you can restore data when needed.

story.title: Not a hoodie in a basement

scenes.text: New joiner Aman imagines hackers as lone geniuses.
The security trainer shows him: most attacks are run like businesses — with call centres, affiliates and targets.

steps.title: Threat actors
steps.body:
- **Cybercriminal groups:** money — ransomware, fraud, data theft for sale.
- **Nation-state groups:** espionage, sabotage, long-term access.
- **Hacktivists:** political or social causes — defacements, leaks, DDoS.
- **Insiders:** current/former staff — malicious (revenge, money) or careless (mistakes).
- **Opportunists:** use ready-made tools against easy targets.

steps.title: Why you are a target
steps.body: Attackers go for the **easiest path**: a person who clicks, reuses a password, approves an MFA prompt, or plugs in an unknown USB. One employee account is often enough to get inside.

steps.title: Solved example: match motive
steps.body:
**Case:** A former employee still has VPN access and deletes project files.
**Actor:** malicious insider. **Motive:** revenge. **Missed control:** timely access removal (offboarding).

steps.title: Solved example: careless insider
steps.body:
**Case:** An analyst uploads a client file to a personal cloud drive to work from home.
**Actor:** careless insider. **Risk:** confidentiality breach. **Fix:** approved tools, data-loss-prevention controls and training.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Only big companies get attacked' — small firms and individuals are hit constantly because defences are weaker.
- Ignoring insiders — many incidents involve human error.

activity.prompt: Match actor to typical goal.

quiz.why: Most cybercrime is financially motivated, so money is the main driver.

quiz.q: An employee emailing data to the wrong person is a:
quiz.why: An employee emailing data to the wrong person is a careless insider incident. It is human error, not an attack.
Attackers usually choose the easiest path in, often a person or weak password rather than the hardest server.

quiz.q: Removing access when staff leave prevents:
quiz.why: Removing access when staff leave prevents insider misuse by former employees. This is an offboarding control.
Hacktivists are motivated by causes or ideology, such as political or social aims.

story.title: The invoice that locked the office

scenes.text: An accounts clerk opens 'Invoice_Overdue.zip' and enables macros in the document inside.
By morning, shared drives show files ending in '.locked' and a ransom note.
Luckily, IT has offline backups tested last month.

steps.title: Types of malware
steps.body:
- **Virus/worm:** spreads by infecting files (virus) or by itself across networks (worm).
- **Trojan:** pretends to be useful, hides malicious functions.
- **Spyware/keylogger/infostealer:** steals passwords, cookies, screenshots.
- **Ransomware:** encrypts data and demands payment; modern gangs also **steal data first** and threaten to leak it ('double extortion').
- **Botnet agent:** enlists the device for attacks.

steps.title: How it gets in
steps.body: Email attachments and links, fake software downloads and cracks, malicious ads, unpatched internet-facing systems (VPNs, servers), stolen remote-access credentials, infected USB drives.

steps.title: Solved example: break the chain
steps.body:
Chain: phishing email → zip → document asks to **enable macros** → malware runs → spreads → encrypts.
**Breaks:** email filtering; block macros from the internet; employee refuses to enable content and reports; endpoint protection; least privilege; segmented network; offline backups for recovery.

steps.title: Solved example: the 3-2-1 backup rule
steps.body: Keep **3** copies of data, on **2** different media, with **1** copy offsite/offline (immutable). Test restores regularly — an untested backup is a hope, not a plan.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Clicking 'Enable editing/Enable content' because a document says so.
- Turning off antivirus because it's 'slow'.
- Trying to clean an infection yourself instead of disconnecting and calling IT.

activity.prompt: Order a typical ransomware attack chain.
items: User opens it and enables macros
Files are encrypted and a ransom note appears

options: Encrypt and threaten to leak stolen data
quiz.why: Double extortion means encrypting data and also threatening to leak stolen data. Restoring from backup then doesn't remove the leak threat.
A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it.
In the 3-2-1 backup rule, the '1' is one offsite or offline copy, which attackers on the network can't reach.

quiz.q: A document asks you to 'Enable content' to view an invoice. You should:
quiz.why: A document asking you to 'Enable content' to see an invoice is a classic macro malware trick. Don't enable it; report it.

options: Disconnect from network and call IT
quiz.why: If you suspect infection, disconnect from the network and call IT to contain the spread. Rebooting or deleting files doesn't help.

scenes.text: A long-time supplier emails: 'We changed banks — please pay this month's ₹18 lakh to the new account.'
The email address looks right; it really is the supplier's mailbox — hacked.
Accounts officer Bhavna calls the supplier on the number in the contract, not the email.

steps.title: Business Email Compromise (BEC)
steps.body: Attackers take over or spoof an email account (a supplier, the CEO, a lawyer) and request payments, gift cards or data. Because there's often **no malware**, filters may miss it. Signs: urgency, secrecy, changed bank details, unusual payment routes.

steps.title: Account takeover
steps.body: Attackers use stolen or guessed passwords (from data breaches, phishing, infostealers) to log in. **Credential stuffing** tries leaked username/password pairs across many sites — which is why reusing passwords is dangerous.

steps.title: Solved example: Bhavna's verification
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Do not use contact details in the suspicious email.
**Step 2:** Call the supplier on a **known number** (contract/vendor master).
**Step 3:** Supplier confirms no change → it's fraud.
**Step 4:** Report to security; warn the supplier their mailbox is compromised; if money was sent, contact the bank immediately and report to 1930/cybercrime.gov.in.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Replying to the same email to 'confirm' — the attacker answers.
- Skipping verification because the CEO 'is in a hurry'.
- Delaying the report after a mistaken payment — speed improves recovery chances.

a.text: The 'CEO' emails: 'Urgent and confidential: buy ₹50,000 of gift cards for a client and send me the codes.' What do you do?

choices.label: Buy them — it's the CEO
Verify through a separate known channel (call or official chat)

b.text: You send codes. The real CEO knows nothing. What now?

choices.label: Report immediately to security and the card issuer
choices.feedback: Fast reporting is the only chance of recovery.

c.text: The CEO's assistant says he never sent it. You report the email to security. They block the sender and warn others.

d.text: Some codes may be blocked if reported fast. Lesson: urgency + secrecy + gift cards = stop and verify.

options: Deception and urgency, often without malware
quiz.why: Business email compromise (BEC) relies on deception and urgency, often without malware.

quiz.q: To verify a bank change request, use:
options: A known phone number from records
quiz.why: Verify a bank change request using a known phone number from your records. Details in the email may belong to the fraudster.
Credential stuffing exploits password reuse: leaked username-password pairs are tried on other sites.

quiz.q: Money sent to fraudsters — report to:
quiz.why: If money went to fraudsters, report to your bank and 1930 immediately. Speed helps freeze the funds.
Gift-card requests from 'executives' are a common fraud red flag, because gift cards are hard to trace.

questions.q: CIA stands for:
questions.why: CIA stands for Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability, the core security triad.

questions.q: Ransomware primarily:
questions.why: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment to unlock it, which is extortion.

questions.q: National cybercrime helpline:
questions.why: India's national cybercrime helpline is 1930. 1098 is Childline and 14416 is Tele-MANAS.

questions.q: Changed vendor bank details should be:
questions.why: Changed vendor bank details should be verified through a known channel, not by replying to the email.

questions.q: An outage due to a traffic flood harms:
questions.why: An outage due to a traffic flood harms availability. This is what a DDoS attack does.

questions.q: Infostealers typically steal:
questions.why: Infostealers typically steal passwords and session cookies, so attackers can access accounts.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Backups help recover from ransomware. Reason (R): Offline backups cannot be encrypted by malware on the network.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: backups help recover from ransomware, and offline backups can't be encrypted by malware on the network.

questions.q: Credential stuffing succeeds mainly because of:
questions.why: Credential stuffing succeeds mainly because people reuse passwords across sites.

questions.q: A former employee's active VPN account is an example of:
questions.why: A former employee's active VPN account is insider risk from poor offboarding, since access wasn't removed.

questions.q: Which control best protects integrity of payments?
questions.why: Dual approval and call-back verification protect payment integrity by preventing unauthorised changes.

questions.q: Case: A zip from an unknown sender contains a document asking to enable macros. Best action?
options: Don't open further; report as phishing
questions.why: A zip from an unknown sender with a document asking to enable macros is a malware delivery trick. Don't open it further; report it as phishing.

questions.q: Case: Ransom note appears. Which is the right first step?
options: Disconnect the device from the network and inform IT/security
questions.why: If a ransom note appears, disconnect the device from the network and inform IT or security, to contain it. Paying or deleting files makes things worse.

questions.q: Case: The supplier's real mailbox was hacked and sends bank-change mail. Which is true?
options: Sender address checks alone won't detect it; verification by known phone is needed
questions.why: If the supplier's real mailbox was hacked, the sender address looks genuine. Verification by a known phone number is needed, since filters and address checks won't catch it.

questions.q: Why is double extortion harder to defeat with backups alone?
options: Data was stolen and may be leaked even if you restore
questions.why: Double extortion is harder to beat with backups alone because data was stolen and may be leaked even if you restore. The confidentiality impact remains.

questions.q: Which combination best reduces ransomware impact?
options: Patching, MFA, least privilege, segmentation, tested offline backups
questions.why: Defence in depth works best: patching, MFA, least privilege, segmentation and tested offline backups. Antivirus or training alone isn't enough.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Phishing and social engineering
courses.summary: The psychology attackers exploit, how to inspect emails and links, phone and SMS scams (vishing, smishing, 'digital arrest'), QR and deepfake tricks, and physical social engineering.
outcomes: Learners can name the persuasion levers in scams
Learners can inspect sender, links and attachments
Learners can recognise vishing, smishing, QR and deepfake scams
Learners can resist tailgating and pretexting
Learners can report phishing correctly

scenes.text: 'Your salary account will be blocked in 2 hours. Verify your KYC now.'
Pooja's heart races. She's about to click.
She remembers: 'If it makes me panic, it's designed to.'

steps.title: Six levers attackers pull
steps.body:
- **Urgency:** 'within 2 hours'
- **Authority:** pretending to be CEO, bank, police, tax department
- **Fear:** account blocked, legal action
- **Greed/reward:** prize, refund, cashback
- **Curiosity:** 'see who viewed your profile', 'salary revision list'
- **Helpfulness/trust:** 'I'm from IT, can you help me test?'

steps.title: The pause rule
steps.body: Strong emotion + a request to click, pay, share or install = **pause**. Verify through a channel **you** choose (official app, known number, typed URL).

steps.title: Solved example: dissect a message
steps.body:
'Dear employee, the HR salary revision list for 2026 is attached. Confidential — view before 5 PM.'
**Levers:** curiosity (salary), urgency (5 PM), authority (HR), secrecy.
**Action:** don't open; check the HR portal directly; report the email.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'I'm too smart to fall for it' — tired, busy people fall for good scams.
- Thinking spelling errors always reveal phishing — many scams are now well written (often with AI).

activity.prompt: Match the line to the lever.

quiz.q: A message creating panic should make you:
quiz.why: A message creating panic should make you pause and verify independently, because emotion is the scammer's weapon.
Verify using a channel you choose, such as a known number, not the numbers or links in the message.

quiz.q: Perfect grammar means a message is:
quiz.why: Perfect grammar doesn't make a message safe. Scams can be polished.

quiz.q: 'This is the CEO' uses which lever?
quiz.why: 'This is the CEO' uses authority to pressure you to comply.
Secrecy requests like 'don't tell anyone' are a red flag, because they isolate the victim from help.

scenes.text: An email from 'Microsoft 365 Security' says Rahul's password expires today.
He hovers over the button: the link goes to micros0ft-login-help.com.
He clicks 'Report phishing' instead.

steps.title: Check the sender
steps.body: Look at the **actual address**, not the display name. 'IT Helpdesk <helpdesk@company-support-desk.com>' is not your company. Watch for look-alike domains: rn vs m, 0 vs o, extra words, different top-level domains. External-sender banners are a useful warning.

steps.title: Read a URL correctly
steps.body: The real domain is the part **just before the first single '/'** after '://', reading right to left from there. In `https://login.microsoft.com.verify-acct.net/secure`, the domain is **verify-acct.net** — not Microsoft. Hover (desktop) or long-press (mobile) to preview links. HTTPS/padlock only means the connection is encrypted, **not** that the site is honest.

steps.title: Solved example: find the real domain
steps.body:
**1)** `https://hr.company.com/payslips` → company.com ✔
**2)** `https://company.com.payslip-view.in/login` → payslip-view.in ✘
**3)** `https://c0mpany.com/login` → c0mpany.com (zero, not o) ✘

steps.title: Risky attachments
steps.body: Be careful with: .zip/.rar/.7z, .html/.htm (fake login pages), .iso/.img, .exe/.scr/.js, Office files asking to enable macros, PDFs with 'click to view document' buttons.

steps.title: Report, don't just delete
steps.body: Use the **Report phishing** button or forward to the security team as instructed. One report can protect everyone who received the same email.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trusting the padlock icon.
- Trusting the display name.
- Entering your password on a page opened from an email link — always go to the site by typing or using a bookmark.

activity.prompt: What is the real domain — safe (company.com) or not?

quiz.q: In https://bank.com.secure-check.co/login the real domain is:
quiz.why: In https://bank.com.secure-check.co/login the real domain is secure-check.co, the registrable domain just before the path. 'bank.com' is only a subdomain label.
The padlock only means the connection is encrypted. It doesn't mean the site is trustworthy or malware-free.

quiz.q: Which attachment is risky for fake logins?
quiz.why: An .html attachment is risky because it can host a fake login page. A CSV you exported or a photo you took is expected and low risk.

quiz.q: The best action for a phishing email:
options: Report it via the official button
quiz.why: Report a phishing email using the official report button, which protects others. Replying, unsubscribing or forwarding can spread the harm.

quiz.q: Display name 'CEO' with a Gmail address is:
quiz.why: A display name of 'CEO' with a Gmail address is suspicious, because display names are easy to fake.

lessons.title: Phone, SMS, QR and deepfake scams

scenes.text: A video call shows a man in police uniform: 'A parcel in your name had drugs. You're under digital arrest. Stay on camera.'
He demands money be moved to a 'verification account'.
Nikhil's sister knows: real police don't arrest people on video calls or ask for money transfers.

steps.title: Vishing and smishing
steps.body:
- **Vishing** = voice phishing: fake bank, courier, customs, police, telecom or tech-support calls.
- **Smishing** = SMS/WhatsApp phishing: 'KYC expiring', 'electricity cut tonight', 'parcel held', 'refund pending'.
- Never share **OTPs**, PINs, CVV or screen-share/remote-access with callers. Banks don't ask for OTPs.

steps.title: 'Digital arrest' scams (India)
steps.body: Fraudsters pose as police, CBI, customs or courts on video calls, claim you're involved in a crime and keep you 'under digital arrest' until you transfer money. **There is no such thing as digital arrest under Indian law.** Hang up, and report on **1930** or **cybercrime.gov.in**.

steps.title: QR and UPI tricks
steps.body: To **receive** money on UPI you never need to scan a QR or enter your PIN. A 'collect request' or QR that asks for your PIN **sends** money from you. Fake QR stickers on parking meters or posters can lead to phishing pages ('quishing').

steps.title: Deepfakes
steps.body: AI can clone voices and faces. A 'boss' on a video call asking for urgent payment may be fake. Use a **verification phrase** or call back on a known number for any money or data request.

steps.title: Solved example: the buyer on a classifieds site
steps.body:
**Case:** A 'buyer' sends a QR saying 'scan to receive ₹15,000'.
**Step 1:** Receiving money never needs PIN → red flag.
**Step 2:** Decline; ask them to pay to your UPI ID.
**Step 3:** Report the profile.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Installing remote-access apps (screen-sharing) on a 'support' caller's request.
- Trusting caller ID — numbers can be spoofed.
- Staying on a threatening call out of fear — hang up and verify.

statements.s: You must enter your UPI PIN to receive money.
Indian police can place you under 'digital arrest' on a video call.
statements.why: No such legal concept — it's a scam.

statements.s: Banks will never ask you for your OTP.
statements.why: Treat any OTP request as fraud.

statements.s: Caller ID can be spoofed.
A voice that sounds exactly like your boss is always your boss.

quiz.why: Smishing is phishing through SMS or messaging apps. Email phishing is just called phishing.

quiz.q: A caller asks for your OTP to 'stop a fraudulent transaction'. You:
options: Refuse and hang up; call your bank on the official number
quiz.why: Never share your OTP. Refuse, hang up and call your bank on its official number, since an OTP authorises transactions.

quiz.q: 'Digital arrest' calls should be reported to:
quiz.why: 'Digital arrest' calls are scams and should be reported to 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.

quiz.q: Entering your UPI PIN on a request:
quiz.why: Entering your UPI PIN on a request sends money from your account. You don't need a PIN to receive money.

quiz.q: Best defence against deepfake 'boss' calls for payments:
options: Call back on a known number / use a verification phrase
quiz.why: Against a deepfake 'boss' call, call back on a known number or use a verification phrase. A face or voice alone can be faked.

scenes.text: A man in a courier T-shirt, carrying boxes, smiles and says 'Hold the door?' at the badge gate.
Polite Shreya almost does. Then she remembers tailgating.
She says, 'Reception will help you sign in,' and points the way.

steps.title: Common tricks
steps.body:
- **Tailgating/piggybacking:** following someone through a secure door.
- **Pretexting:** a made-up story — 'I'm the auditor', 'I'm from the AC company'.
- **Baiting:** leaving infected USB drives labelled 'Salary 2026'.
- **Shoulder surfing:** watching screens or keypads.
- **Dumpster diving:** reading discarded printouts.

steps.title: Solved example: the 'IT technician'
steps.body:
**Case:** A visitor says, 'I'm here to fix your laptop — log in for me.'
**Step 1:** Is there a ticket? Ask for the ticket number and check with IT via the helpdesk.
**Step 2:** Never hand over your logged-in device or password.
**Step 3:** If unverified, escort to reception and inform security.

steps.title: Simple habits
steps.body: Badge every time; don't hold doors to secure areas; lock your screen (Windows+L / Ctrl+Cmd+Q); clean desk; shred sensitive printouts; never plug in found USBs — hand them to IT.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Being 'too polite' to challenge someone — challenge kindly and redirect to reception.
- Leaving passwords on sticky notes.

a.text: You find a USB drive labelled 'Bonus list 2026' in the cafeteria. What do you do?

choices.label: Plug it in to find the owner
Hand it to IT/security without plugging it in

b.text: Your laptop shows a strange window and then freezes. What now?

choices.label: Disconnect from the network and call IT immediately

c.text: IT confirms it was part of a test — you passed. Unknown USBs can carry malware that runs on connection.

d.text: IT isolates your laptop. Lesson: never plug in unknown media.

options: Following someone through a secure door
quiz.why: Tailgating is following someone through a secure door without using your own badge. It is a physical access trick.

quiz.q: A found USB drive should be:
quiz.why: A found USB drive should be handed to IT unplugged. Plugging it in is a baiting risk.

options: A made-up story to gain trust
quiz.why: Pretexting uses a made-up story to gain trust and get information or access.
Lock your screen whenever you step away, to prevent misuse of your session.

quiz.q: Someone without a badge asks you to hold the secure door:
quiz.why: Politely direct the person to reception. Holding the door lets an unverified person in.

questions.q: Phishing via SMS is called:
questions.why: Phishing via SMS is called smishing. Vishing is by voice and whaling targets senior executives.

questions.q: Banks ask for your OTP over phone:
questions.why: Banks never ask for your OTP over the phone. Anyone asking for it is likely a fraudster.

questions.q: Tailgating is a:
questions.why: Tailgating is a physical social engineering trick, where someone follows an authorised person through a secure door. It isn't a virus, firewall or backup.

questions.q: The padlock icon proves:
questions.why: The padlock proves only that the connection is encrypted. It doesn't show the site is official, safe or free of malware.

questions.q: Which lever is 'Reply within 15 minutes'?
questions.why: 'Reply within 15 minutes' uses urgency, time pressure that stops you thinking and verifying.

questions.q: UPI PIN is needed to:
questions.why: A UPI PIN is needed to send money, because it authorises a debit. You don't need it to receive money.

questions.q: Real domain in https://secure.hdfc.com.kyc-update.top/x is:
questions.why: In https://secure.hdfc.com.kyc-update.top/x the real domain is kyc-update.top, the registrable domain just before the path. 'hdfc.com' is only part of a subdomain.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 'Digital arrest' is a scam. Reason (R): Indian law has no procedure of arresting someone over a video call and demanding transfers.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: 'digital arrest' is a scam because Indian law has no procedure for arresting someone over a video call or demanding transfers.

questions.q: HTML attachments in unexpected emails are risky because:
options: They often open fake login pages
questions.why: HTML attachments in unexpected emails often open fake login pages, which harvest credentials.

questions.q: Baiting uses:
questions.why: Baiting uses infected media or tempting downloads, such as a dropped USB drive, as lures.

questions.q: Case: You entered your password on a fake page 10 minutes ago. Best steps?
options: Change password from the real site, report to security, check MFA/sign-ins
questions.why: Change your password from the real site, report it to security and check MFA and sign-ins. This contains an account takeover; waiting or deleting only the email isn't enough.

questions.q: Case: A video call with your 'CFO' asks you to wire ₹40 lakh secretly. The video looks real. Best action?
options: Verify via a known number or in person; follow payment approvals
questions.why: A deepfake can make a video call look real, so verify through a known number or in person and follow payment approvals. Never pay secretly on a call alone.

questions.q: Case: A 'bank officer' asks you to install a screen-sharing app to block a fraud. Correct?
options: Hang up; call the bank via official number
questions.why: Hang up and call the bank on its official number. Installing a screen-sharing app or sharing an OTP gives scammers control of your device and money.

questions.q: Which is the BEST single habit against phishing links?
options: Navigate to sites yourself (bookmark/app) rather than via message links
questions.why: The best single habit is to go to sites yourself, via a bookmark or app, rather than through message links. That avoids deceptive links.

questions.q: Why is reporting a phishing email better than deleting it?
options: Security can block it for everyone and investigate
It deletes it for you only
questions.why: Reporting a phishing email lets security block it for everyone and investigate, while deleting protects only you.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Passwords, MFA, passkeys and identity
courses.summary: Why length beats complexity, password managers, multi-factor authentication types and their strength, MFA fatigue and SIM-swap attacks, passkeys, and least privilege.
outcomes: Learners can create long, unique passphrases
Learners can explain why password managers help
Learners can rank MFA methods by phishing resistance
Learners can respond to MFA fatigue and SIM-swap signs
Learners can apply least privilege to their own access

scenes.text: Kunal's password is 'Summer@2026' — it meets the rules: capital, number, symbol.
It also appears in attackers' guess lists within seconds.
His friend shows him a password manager and a four-word passphrase.

steps.title: Length beats complexity
steps.body: Modern guidance (e.g. NIST SP 800-63B) favours **long passwords or passphrases**, checking new passwords against lists of breached/common ones, and **not forcing periodic changes** unless there's evidence of compromise. 'Summer@2026' is complex-looking but predictable. 'tiger-lantern-monsoon-pencil' is long and random.

steps.title: Why length works (maths)
steps.body:
Possible combinations = (characters available)^(length).
- 8 lowercase letters: 26⁸ ≈ 2.1 × 10¹¹
- 4 random words from a 7,776-word list: 7776⁴ ≈ 3.7 × 10¹⁵
Each random word from 7,776 adds about **12.9 bits** of entropy (log₂ 7776 ≈ 12.9). Four words ≈ 51.7 bits; six words ≈ 77.5 bits.

steps.title: Solved example: entropy
steps.body:
**Q:** Bits of entropy for 5 random words from a 7,776-word list?
**Step 1:** bits per word = log₂(7776) ≈ 12.92.
**Step 2:** 5 × 12.92 ≈ **64.6 bits**.
**Note:** the words must be chosen **randomly** (dice or a generator), not a famous phrase.

steps.title: Password managers
steps.body: A password manager generates and stores a **unique** strong password for every site, autofills only on the real domain (helping against phishing), and needs you to remember just one strong master passphrase (protected with MFA). Use the one your company approves for work.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reusing one password everywhere — one breach unlocks all.
- Patterns like Name@123, Company#2026, keyboard walks (qwerty123).
- Storing passwords in an unprotected spreadsheet or sticky note.

activity.prompt: About how many bits of entropy do 6 random words from a 7,776-word list give? (log₂7776 ≈ 12.92)

options: four random unrelated words with separators
quiz.why: Four random unrelated words with separators give a long, random passphrase. 'Qwerty123$', 'P@ssw0rd!' and 'Summer@2026' follow predictable patterns.

quiz.q: Forced password changes every 30 days are:
options: Not recommended without evidence of compromise
quiz.why: Forced 30-day password changes aren't recommended without evidence of compromise, because they lead to predictable patterns like adding a number.

quiz.q: Main benefit of a password manager:
options: Unique strong passwords for every site
quiz.why: A password manager lets you use a unique strong password for every site. It doesn't replace MFA.

quiz.q: Bits per random word from 7,776 words:
quiz.why: Each random word from a list of 7,776 gives log₂(7776) ≈ 12.9 bits of entropy.
Reusing passwords enables credential stuffing, where leaked pairs are tried on other sites.

scenes.text: Leena's password was phished last month.
But the attacker couldn't log in — her account needed a second factor she controlled.

steps.title: Three factor types
steps.body:
- **Something you know:** password, PIN
- **Something you have:** phone app, hardware key, smart card
- **Something you are:** fingerprint, face
MFA = **two or more different types**. A password + security question is *not* MFA (both 'know').

steps.title: MFA strength (weakest → strongest)
steps.body:
1) SMS/voice codes (vulnerable to SIM swap and phishing)
2) Authenticator app codes (TOTP) — better, but can be phished in real time
3) Push approval with **number matching** — resists blind approvals
4) **FIDO2 security keys / passkeys** — **phishing-resistant**, bound to the real website

steps.title: Solved example: is it MFA?
steps.body:
**a)** Password + OTP via SMS → know + have → MFA ✔ (weaker type)
**b)** Password + mother's maiden name → know + know → ✘
**c)** Fingerprint unlocking a passkey on your phone → are + have → ✔ (strong)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Turning MFA off because it's 'annoying'.
- Reading MFA codes to anyone who calls.
- Using SMS when a stronger method is available for critical accounts (email, bank, admin).

activity.prompt: Order MFA methods from weakest to strongest against phishing.

quiz.why: Password plus a security question is not MFA, because both are 'something you know', the same factor type.
A FIDO2 key or passkey is the most phishing-resistant, because it is bound to the real website. SMS and email codes can be phished.
A fingerprint is a biometric, so it is something you are.

quiz.q: SMS codes are weaker mainly due to:
quiz.why: SMS codes are weaker mainly because of SIM swap, interception and phishing, which are telecom-based attacks.

quiz.q: Someone calls asking for your MFA code:
quiz.why: Never share your MFA code with anyone, even someone who says they are from IT. The code is the access.

lessons.title: MFA fatigue, SIM swap and passkeys

scenes.text: At midnight, Varsha's phone buzzes with login approval prompts — again and again.
Half asleep, she's tempted to tap 'Approve' to make it stop.
She taps 'Deny', then reports it: someone has her password.

steps.title: MFA fatigue (push bombing)
steps.body: Attackers with your password trigger repeated push prompts hoping you approve one. Sometimes they call pretending to be IT: 'Please approve to stop the alerts.' **Unexpected prompt = someone has your password.** Deny, report, and change your password.

steps.title: SIM swap
steps.body: Fraudsters trick or bribe a telecom store to move your number to their SIM, then receive your SMS OTPs. Signs: phone suddenly shows **no network**, messages about SIM change. Act fast: contact your telecom operator and bank; move important accounts off SMS MFA.

steps.title: Passkeys
steps.body: A **passkey** replaces the password with a cryptographic key pair: the private key stays on your device (unlocked by fingerprint, face or PIN) and the website stores only the public key. Because the key works **only on the genuine site's domain**, a fake look-alike site can't trick it — making passkeys **phishing-resistant**. Nothing reusable is stored on the server for attackers to steal.

steps.title: Solved example: incident response for push bombing
steps.body: **Step 1:** Deny all prompts. **Step 2:** Report to security. **Step 3:** Change password from a trusted device. **Step 4:** Review recent sign-ins and sessions; sign out others. **Step 5:** Ask IT about enabling number matching or a security key.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Approving 'just to stop the noise'.
- Ignoring sudden loss of mobile signal.
- Thinking a passkey means 'no security' because there's no password — it's stronger.

statements.s: An unexpected MFA prompt means someone may know your password.
Approving a prompt to make it stop is safe.
Passkeys work on look-alike phishing sites.
statements.why: They are bound to the real domain.

statements.s: Sudden 'No service' on your phone can signal a SIM swap.

quiz.why: MFA fatigue attacks rely on users approving repeated prompts just to stop them, which is called push bombing.

options: You must type a number shown on the login screen
quiz.why: Number matching requires you to type a number shown on the login screen. This prevents blind approval of a prompt.

quiz.q: In a passkey, the server stores:
quiz.why: With a passkey, the server stores only the public key. The private key stays on your device.
A SIM swap hijacks your phone number, so it mainly defeats SMS-based OTP. Hardware keys and passkeys don't depend on the number.

quiz.q: After denying unexpected prompts you should:
quiz.why: After denying unexpected prompts, change your password and report it. The prompts mean someone has your password.

scenes.text: At a growing startup, every developer is a cloud admin 'to move fast'.
One phished laptop lets an attacker delete production databases.
The new security lead introduces least privilege.

steps.title: Least privilege
steps.body: Give each person and system **only the access needed**, for **only as long as needed**. Use separate admin accounts for admin tasks, time-limited elevation (just-in-time access), and regular **access reviews**.

steps.title: Joiner–mover–leaver
steps.body:
- **Joiner:** access based on role.
- **Mover:** remove old access when changing teams (avoid 'privilege creep').
- **Leaver:** disable all accounts on the last day, recover devices, rotate shared secrets.

steps.title: Solved example: review your own access
steps.body:
Riya moved from Finance to Marketing 6 months ago.
**Check:** she still has access to payroll folders → privilege creep.
**Action:** request removal; manager confirms in quarterly access review.

steps.title: Account hygiene
steps.body:
- Don't share accounts or passwords — even with your manager.
- Use separate work and personal accounts.
- Sign out of shared/public computers.
- Review connected apps and active sessions monthly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using an admin account for email and browsing.
- Sharing a single team login so nobody knows who did what.

activity.prompt: Identity hygiene checklist
items: Every account has a unique password (via manager)
MFA enabled on email, bank and work accounts
Phishing-resistant MFA or passkey on the most critical accounts
I requested removal of access I no longer need
I reviewed active sessions and connected apps

options: Only the access needed, only as long as needed
quiz.why: Least privilege means only the access needed, only as long as needed. It limits the damage from a compromised account.

options: Old access isn't removed after role changes
quiz.why: Privilege creep happens when old access isn't removed after role changes, so permissions accumulate.

quiz.q: Using admin accounts for browsing is:
quiz.why: Using admin accounts for browsing is risky, because any malware you meet then runs with admin rights.
Shared team logins hurt accountability, since you can't tell who did what.
On a leaver's last day, disable their accounts and recover devices. Keeping access or sharing passwords creates insider risk.

questions.q: Which factor type is a hardware key?
questions.why: A hardware key is something you have, a possession factor. Passwords are something you know and fingerprints are something you are.

questions.q: Best password approach:
questions.why: A long, unique passphrase per site is best. Reusing the same password or using predictable ones like Name@123 is weak.

questions.q: Unexpected MFA prompts should be:
questions.why: Unexpected MFA prompts should be denied and reported, since they could mean someone has your password (push bombing).

questions.q: Password + PIN is:
questions.why: Password plus PIN is not MFA, because both are 'something you know'.

questions.q: Most phishing-resistant MFA:
questions.why: A FIDO2 key or passkey is the most phishing-resistant MFA because it is bound to the real origin.

questions.q: Least privilege reduces:
questions.why: Least privilege reduces the damage from a compromised account, giving a smaller blast radius.

questions.q: Entropy of 4 random words (7,776 list):
questions.why: Entropy for 4 random words from 7,776 is 4 × 12.92 ≈ 51.7 bits.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Passkeys resist phishing. Reason (R): The private key only signs for the genuine site's domain.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: a passkey's private key signs only for the genuine site's domain, so a fake site can't use it.

questions.q: SIM swap sign:
questions.why: A sudden loss of mobile network can be a sign of a SIM swap, because your number has moved to another SIM.

questions.q: Number matching protects against:
questions.why: Number matching protects against MFA fatigue, since it forces a deliberate action instead of a blind tap.

questions.q: How many combinations for an 8-character lowercase password?
questions.why: With 26 letters and 8 positions, combinations = 26⁸ ≈ 2.1 × 10¹¹, as characters raised to the length.

questions.q: Case: 'IT' calls saying 'approve the prompt I'm sending to fix your account'. You:
options: Refuse; report; IT never needs your approval this way
questions.why: Refuse and report. IT never needs you to approve a prompt this way, and it is social engineering combined with MFA fatigue.

questions.q: Case: You changed teams; you still access old payroll folders. Best action?
questions.why: Request removal of old access you no longer need, to fix privilege creep. Keeping or sharing it adds risk.

questions.q: Which statement about NIST-style password guidance is correct?
options: Screen against breached passwords; avoid forced periodic resets without cause
questions.why: Modern NIST-style guidance says screen passwords against breached lists and avoid forced periodic resets without cause. Monthly changes and banning managers are outdated.

questions.q: Why can a real-time phishing proxy steal an authenticator app code but not a passkey login?
options: The code is just a number the user types anywhere; the passkey signature is bound to the real origin
questions.why: An authenticator code is just a number the user can type into any site, so a proxy can relay it. A passkey signature is bound to the real origin, so the proxy can't reuse it.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Safe devices, networks, data and incident response
courses.summary: Updates and endpoint protection, safe Wi-Fi and VPN use, working from home and travel, handling and classifying data (including AI tools), and how to report and respond to incidents in India.
outcomes: Learners can keep devices patched and protected
Learners can use public Wi-Fi and VPNs safely
Learners can classify and handle data correctly, including with AI tools
Learners can report incidents quickly through the right channels

lessons.title: Updates, endpoint protection and safe software

scenes.text: Ravi has clicked 'Remind me tomorrow' on updates for three weeks.
An attacker exploits a browser flaw that was fixed in the update he skipped.

steps.title: Why patch
steps.body: Updates fix **vulnerabilities** — flaws attackers can exploit. Once a patch is public, attackers study it and target unpatched devices within days. Update OS, browser, apps and router firmware promptly; restart when asked.

steps.title: Endpoint protection
steps.body: Keep antivirus/EDR on, disk encryption enabled (BitLocker/FileVault), screen lock with short timeout, and firewall on. Don't disable security tools.

steps.title: Solved example: the cracked software
steps.body:
**Case:** a colleague offers a 'free' cracked design tool.
**Risk:** cracks often bundle infostealers.
**Action:** decline; request a licence through IT's approved software catalogue.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Postponing updates for weeks.
- Installing browser extensions that ask to 'read and change all data on all websites' without need.
- Using unsupported (end-of-life) operating systems.

activity.prompt: Device health check
items: Screen lock after 5 minutes or less

quiz.why: Patches fix vulnerabilities, which are security flaws attackers can exploit.
Cracked software often comes with bundled malware such as infostealers.
Disk encryption protects data on a lost or stolen laptop, keeping data at rest confidential.
An end-of-life OS no longer gets security fixes, so new vulnerabilities remain open.

quiz.q: Browser extension asking to read all website data should be:
quiz.why: A browser extension asking to read all website data is over-privileged, so avoid it unless essential and approved.

scenes.text: At the airport, Meghna sees two networks: 'Airport_Free_WiFi' and 'Airport Free WiFi 5G'.
One could be an attacker's 'evil twin'.
She uses her phone hotspot and the company VPN instead.

steps.title: Public Wi-Fi risks
steps.body: Fake 'evil twin' hotspots and captive portals that ask for logins. Prefer your **mobile hotspot**; if using public Wi-Fi, connect to the **company VPN**, check you're on HTTPS, and don't install anything a portal asks.

steps.title: Home office
steps.body: Change router default admin password, use WPA2/WPA3, update router firmware, keep work devices for work only, lock screen when family is around, and use headphones for confidential calls.

steps.title: Solved example: travel checklist
steps.body:
**Before:** update devices; enable find-my-device; carry minimal data.
**During:** hotspot or VPN; privacy screen; keep devices with you; don't charge from unknown USB ports (use your own adapter or a data-blocker).
**After:** report any lost device immediately.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving a laptop in the car or hotel lobby.
- Taking calls about deals in public places.
- Delaying the report of a lost device until 'I've searched properly'.

statements.s: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the company network over public Wi-Fi.
Two similarly named hotspots are always safe.
You should report a lost work phone immediately.
Router default passwords are fine to keep.

quiz.why: An evil twin is a fake Wi-Fi hotspot that impersonates a real network to capture traffic.
Your own mobile hotspot is safer than public Wi-Fi because you control it. Open networks, unknown USB and shared PCs are risky.
A home router should use WPA2 or WPA3 encryption. WEP, no password or default admin passwords are weak.

quiz.q: Charging from unknown USB ports risks:
quiz.why: Charging from unknown USB ports risks data access or malware, called juice jacking, because USB carries data too.
Report a lost device immediately so it can be remotely wiped and accounts secured.

scenes.text: Tara pastes a confidential client contract into a free public AI chatbot to get a summary.
Her company's policy allows only an approved enterprise AI tool for confidential data.

steps.title: Typical classification levels
steps.body:
- **Public:** press releases, website content
- **Internal:** org charts, internal announcements
- **Confidential:** client data, contracts, financials, source code
- **Restricted:** highly sensitive personal data, credentials, M&A plans
Higher levels need stronger controls: encryption, limited sharing, approved tools only.

steps.title: Using AI safely
steps.body: Public AI tools may store prompts or use them to improve models. Use only **company-approved** AI tools for internal or confidential data; never paste credentials, personal data or client secrets into unapproved tools; check outputs for errors before using them.

steps.title: Solved example: classify and choose a tool
steps.body:
**Data:** list of customer names and phone numbers → Confidential (personal data).
**Task:** deduplicate. **Tool:** approved spreadsheet or enterprise AI with data protections — not a public chatbot or personal email.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'It's just a summary' — the input is what leaks.
- Sharing files with 'anyone with the link'.
- Emailing confidential files to personal accounts to work at home.

activity.prompt: Classify the data.

items.text: Job ad on the careers page

quiz.why: Client contracts are usually confidential, as they contain sensitive commercial information.

quiz.q: Pasting confidential data into an unapproved public AI tool:
options: Risks data leakage and breaks policy
quiz.why: Pasting confidential data into an unapproved public AI tool risks data leakage and breaks policy, because the data leaves your control.
Higher classification means stronger controls, so protection is proportionate to sensitivity.
Credentials are restricted, the highest sensitivity level.
AI outputs should be checked before use, since they may contain errors.

lessons.title: Incident response and reporting in India

scenes.text: Arjun realises the 'shared document' he opened asked for his password — and he entered it.
He's embarrassed and considers staying quiet.
He reports in 5 minutes. Security resets his account before the attacker logs in.

steps.title: What counts as an incident
steps.body: Clicked a suspicious link or entered credentials; unexpected MFA prompts; malware alerts; lost or stolen device; data sent to the wrong person; strange account activity; ransom notes; suspicious calls asking for data.

steps.title: Employee steps
steps.body:
1) **Stop** — don't keep interacting.
2) **Disconnect** the device from the network if malware is suspected (don't switch off unless told — evidence matters).
3) **Report immediately** to IT/security through the official channel.
4) **Preserve** evidence: don't delete emails or messages.
5) **Follow instructions** — password reset, device handover.

steps.title: Reporting in India
steps.body:
- Organisations: **CERT-In** (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) directions of April 2022 require specified cyber incidents to be reported to CERT-In **within 6 hours** of noticing them. Your security team handles this — which is why they need your report fast.
- Individuals: report cybercrime at **cybercrime.gov.in** or call **1930** (especially for financial fraud — fast reporting can help freeze funds). For immediate danger: **112**.
- Personal data breaches also have duties under the **DPDP Act, 2023**.

steps.title: Solved example: wrong recipient
steps.body:
**Case:** you emailed a spreadsheet of 300 employees' salaries to an external vendor by mistake.
**Step 1:** Try recall (if available) and ask the recipient in writing to delete it and confirm.
**Step 2:** Report to security/privacy immediately with details (time, recipient, data).
**Step 3:** They assess whether it's a reportable personal data breach.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hiding mistakes out of embarrassment — speed matters more than blame; good companies have a no-blame reporting culture.
- Trying to investigate yourself.
- Wiping the device before security sees it.

activity.prompt: Order the employee's incident steps.
items: Stop interacting with the suspicious item
Disconnect from the network if malware is suspected

quiz.q: CERT-In directions require organisations to report specified incidents within:
quiz.why: CERT-In's directions require organisations to report specified cyber incidents within 6 hours (April 2022 directions).

quiz.q: Financial cyber fraud victims should call:
quiz.why: Victims of financial cyber fraud should call the national helpline 1930 immediately.

quiz.q: If you entered your password on a fake page, the first action is:
options: Report immediately and reset via official site
quiz.why: If you entered your password on a fake page, report it immediately and reset it via the official site. Waiting gives attackers time.

quiz.q: Why not wipe a suspected infected device yourself?
quiz.why: Don't wipe a suspected infected device yourself, because the evidence is lost and investigators need it.

quiz.q: Good security culture treats honest mistakes:
quiz.why: A good security culture treats honest mistakes with no blame and fast reporting. Punishment makes people hide incidents.

questions.q: Updates mainly:
questions.why: Updates mainly fix security vulnerabilities (patches), not just colours or speed.

questions.q: Lost laptop should be:
questions.why: A lost laptop should be reported immediately so it can be remotely wiped and credentials changed.

questions.q: Individuals report cybercrime at:
questions.why: Individuals report cybercrime at cybercrime.gov.in, the national portal.

questions.q: VPN on public Wi-Fi:
options: Encrypts traffic to the company network
questions.why: A VPN on public Wi-Fi encrypts traffic to the company network. It doesn't replace antivirus or make you invisible.

questions.q: Customer phone lists are:
questions.why: Customer phone lists are confidential personal data and need protection.

questions.q: Evil twin attack targets:
questions.why: An evil twin attack targets Wi-Fi users with a fake hotspot.

questions.q: CERT-In incident reporting window:
questions.why: CERT-In's incident reporting window is 6 hours.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Report clicking a bad link immediately even if embarrassed. Reason (R): Early reporting lets security contain the attack.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: report a bad click immediately even if embarrassed, because early reporting lets security contain the attack.

questions.q: Pasting source code into an unapproved public AI tool is mainly a:
questions.why: Pasting source code into an unapproved public AI tool is mainly a confidentiality risk, because it leaks the code.

questions.q: Disk encryption helps when:
options: A device is lost or stolen
questions.why: Disk encryption helps when a device is lost or stolen, protecting data at rest. It doesn't stop phishing or DDoS.

questions.q: Case: A malware alert pops up. Best action?
options: Disconnect from network, don't switch off, report
questions.why: Disconnect from the network, don't switch off, and report. This contains the malware while preserving evidence.

questions.q: Case: You sent salary data to the wrong external address. Which is NOT a good step?
options: Ask recipient to delete and confirm
Wait to see if anyone notices
questions.why: Waiting to see if anyone notices is not a good step, since delay harms. Ask the recipient to delete, record the details and report to privacy or security.

questions.q: Case: You lost ₹30,000 to a UPI scam 20 minutes ago. Best action?
questions.why: Call 1930 and your bank immediately. Early reporting in the golden hour can help freeze the funds.

questions.q: Why do security teams prefer you not switch off a compromised machine unless told?
options: Volatile evidence in memory may be lost
questions.why: Switching off a compromised machine may lose volatile evidence in memory that forensics need.

questions.q: Which combination best protects a travelling employee?
options: Updated, encrypted device + hotspot/VPN + privacy screen + immediate loss reporting
questions.why: Layered habits protect a travelling employee: an updated, encrypted device, a hotspot or VPN, a privacy screen and immediate loss reporting. Public Wi-Fi without a lock and unattended laptops are risky.

courses.title: Cybersecurity · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: A one-page summary of the whole course, a mixed phishing-spotting drill, and a full mock test.
outcomes: Learners can recall core rules and numbers
Learners can spot red flags across channels
Learners can score 80%+ on the mock

scenes.text: Security week: Neha designs a one-page poster for her floor.
Everything an employee needs fits on it.

steps.title: Foundations
steps.body:
- CIA: confidentiality, integrity, availability
- Actors: criminals (money), nation-states (espionage), hacktivists (causes), insiders
- Ransomware: encrypt + leak; 3-2-1 backups; patch; least privilege

steps.title: Phishing
steps.body:
- Levers: urgency, authority, fear, reward, curiosity, trust
- Read the real domain; padlock ≠ safe; report don't delete
- Vishing/smishing; no OTP sharing; UPI PIN only to send; no 'digital arrest'

steps.title: Identity
steps.body:
- Long unique passphrases + password manager
- MFA strength: SMS < app < push with number matching < FIDO2/passkey
- Deny unexpected prompts; watch for SIM swap; least privilege

steps.title: Devices & incidents
steps.body:
- Update, encrypt, lock, approved software
- Hotspot/VPN; evil twins; report lost devices
- Classify data; approved AI tools only
- Report fast; CERT-In 6 hours (organisations); 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in; 112

quiz.why: A passkey is the strongest MFA of these because it is phishing-resistant. SMS, email and security questions are weaker.

quiz.q: Report organisational incidents to CERT-In within:
quiz.why: Report organisational incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours under its directions.
In the 3-2-1 backup rule, the '2' means two different media types.

quiz.q: Receiving money on UPI needs your PIN:
quiz.why: You never need a UPI PIN to receive money. The PIN is only to pay.

scenes.text: The trainer shows a mixed inbox.
Teams race to sort real from fake.

steps.title: Message 1
steps.body: 'Your parcel is held; pay ₹25 fee: bit.ly/xyz' → shortened link + small fee → **scam**.

steps.title: Message 2
steps.body: Calendar invite from your manager's real account for your weekly 1:1, no links/attachments beyond the usual meeting → **likely legitimate**.

steps.title: Message 3
steps.body: 'IT: your mailbox is full, log in at mailbox-company.help' → look-alike domain → **phishing**.

steps.title: Message 4
steps.body: Call from 'TRAI' saying your number will be disconnected unless you press 9 → **scam** (pressure + authority).

steps.title: The 3-question test
steps.body: 1) Is it expected? 2) Does it push emotion or urgency? 3) Does it ask me to click, pay, share or install? Two 'yes' → verify independently.

activity.prompt: Likely scam or likely legitimate?

items.text: Payslip notice in the official HR portal you logged into yourself
WhatsApp from unknown number: 'Hi Dad, new number, need money urgently'
Expected IT change notice on the intranet
'You won a lottery you never entered'

quiz.q: 'Hi Mum, new number, send money' is a:
quiz.why: 'Hi Mum, new number, send money' is a common impersonation scam. Verify by calling the old number.

quiz.q: Shortened links in unexpected SMS are:
quiz.why: Shortened links in unexpected SMS are suspicious because they hide the destination.
The 3-question test starts with 'Is it expected?', since context is the first check.

quiz.q: Logging into the portal yourself is safer because:
quiz.why: Logging into the portal yourself is safer because you avoid deceptive links and control the destination.

scenes.text: Take the full mock under time.
Revisit lessons for any wrong area.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body: For case questions, choose the answer that **contains, reports and verifies** — not the one that ignores, hides or 'fixes it yourself'.

steps.title: Numbers & names to recall
steps.body: 6 hours (CERT-In) · 1930 · 112 · 12.9 bits/word (7,776 list) · 3-2-1 · FIDO2 · WPA2/WPA3

steps.title: Keep learning
steps.body: Security changes fast. Read your company's security bulletins and update habits at least yearly.

activity.prompt: Which cyber habit will you change this week, and how?
activity.hint: e.g. set up a password manager, enable passkeys on email, turn on auto-updates.

quiz.why: The best case-answer pattern is contain, report, verify. Ignoring, hiding or fixing silently is wrong.
Use WPA2 or WPA3 for home Wi-Fi. Open networks and WEP are weak.
India's emergency number is 112.

questions.q: Availability is harmed by:
questions.why: Ransomware encrypting servers harms availability, as systems become unusable.

questions.q: Never share your:
questions.why: Never share your OTP, because it authorises access or payments.

questions.q: Found USB:
questions.why: A found USB drive should be handed to IT, not plugged in. Plugging it in is a baiting risk.

questions.q: Phishing via voice:
questions.why: Phishing by voice is vishing. Smishing is SMS, quishing is QR codes and whaling targets executives.

questions.q: Password manager benefit:
questions.why: A password manager's benefit is unique passwords everywhere. It doesn't remove MFA or updates.

questions.q: Padlock icon guarantees:
questions.why: The padlock icon guarantees only encryption of the connection, not honesty or safety.

questions.q: Least privilege:
questions.why: Least privilege means giving the minimum access needed.

questions.q: QR to 'receive money' asking for PIN:
questions.why: A QR to 'receive money' that asks for your PIN is a scam, because a PIN sends money.

questions.q: Real domain in https://login.company.com.evil.io/a:
questions.why: In https://login.company.com.evil.io/a the real domain is evil.io, the registrable domain at the right before the path.

questions.q: Assertion (A): SMS OTP is the strongest MFA. Reason (R): SIM swaps can redirect SMS.
questions.why: The assertion is false: SMS OTP is among the weakest MFA. The reason is true, since SIM swaps can redirect SMS.

questions.q: Double-extortion ransomware threatens:
questions.why: Double-extortion ransomware threatens both encryption and a data leak.

questions.q: Entropy of 5 random words (7,776 list):
questions.why: Entropy for 5 random words from 7,776 is 5 × 12.92 ≈ 64.6 bits.

questions.q: Case: Supplier email requests new bank details; the email is from their genuine domain. Best action?
options: Call supplier on known number before changing
questions.why: Call the supplier on a known number before changing details. The supplier's genuine mailbox may have been compromised, so replying doesn't verify.

questions.q: Case: 30 MFA prompts arrive at 2 a.m. Best action?
questions.why: Deny the prompts, report it and change your password. Repeated prompts mean someone has your password; approving one would let them in.

questions.q: Case: Colleague pastes client data into a free AI chatbot. Main issue?
questions.why: Pasting client data into a free AI chatbot is mainly a confidentiality problem and a policy breach, since the data leaves your control.

questions.q: Case: You notice you have no mobile signal and then get a 'SIM changed' message. Best action?
options: Contact operator and bank immediately; secure accounts
questions.why: No signal followed by a 'SIM changed' message suggests a SIM swap. Contact the operator and bank immediately and secure your accounts.

questions.q: Which is phishing-resistant because it's bound to the website's origin?
questions.why: A passkey or FIDO2 key is phishing-resistant because it is bound to the website's origin. SMS, TOTP and security questions are not.

questions.q: Which best explains why attackers target employees rather than servers?
options: Humans are often the easiest path; one account can open the door
questions.why: Attackers target employees because humans are often the easiest path, and one account can open the door.

questions.q: Which ordering is correct for an employee who suspects malware?
options: Stop → disconnect → report → preserve → follow instructions
questions.why: The correct order for suspected malware is stop, disconnect, report, preserve and follow instructions. Wiping or rebooting destroys evidence.

corp-finlit.title: Money for employees: salary, PF, tax and investing (India)
corp-finlit.description: Chapter-by-chapter financial literacy for Indian employees: CTC and salary slips, PF, NPS, gratuity and insurance, old vs new income-tax regimes, budgeting and debt, and investing basics.

courses.title: Ch 1 · CTC, salary structure and your payslip
courses.summary: Why CTC is not your in-hand salary, every common salary component and deduction, how to read a payslip line by line, and how to compare job offers.
outcomes: Learners can explain CTC, gross salary and net (in-hand) pay
Learners can describe basic, HRA, special allowance, LTA and variable pay
Learners can compute in-hand pay from a payslip
Learners can compare two offers on fixed pay, benefits and risks

scenes.text: Ritu gets an offer of ₹12 lakh CTC and plans a ₹30,000 rent assuming ₹1 lakh a month.
Her first salary credit is about ₹77,000.
Her senior explains the three layers of salary.

steps.title: Three numbers
steps.body:
- **CTC (cost to company):** everything the employer spends on you in a year — fixed pay, **employer PF contribution**, **gratuity provision**, insurance premiums, variable/bonus (often at 100% target), sometimes meal cards and other benefits.
- **Gross salary:** what appears as earnings on your payslip before deductions (basic, HRA, allowances).
- **Net / in-hand / take-home:** gross minus deductions (employee PF, professional tax, income tax TDS, others).

steps.title: Solved example: Ritu's ₹12 lakh
steps.body:
Annual CTC ₹12,00,000 =
- Variable pay (paid yearly, if targets met): ₹1,00,000
- Employer PF (12% of basic ₹4,80,000): ₹57,600
- Gratuity provision (4.81% of basic): ≈ ₹23,088
- Group insurance: ₹9,312
- **Fixed gross** (rest): ₹10,10,000 → **₹84,167/month**
Monthly deductions: employee PF ₹4,800, professional tax ₹200, TDS (depends on regime) — so **in-hand ≈ ₹75,000–₹79,000** in most months (variable comes separately).

steps.title: Ask HR these questions
steps.body:
- What is the **fixed** component per month?
- Is variable pay guaranteed? How was it paid last year?
- Is employer PF and gratuity **inside** CTC?
- Any joining bonus clawback if I leave early?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing CTC by 12 to plan spending.
- Treating target variable pay as guaranteed.
- Ignoring that gratuity is paid only after eligible service (usually 5 years under the 1972 Act).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not financial or tax advice. Company structures differ; check your offer letter and payslip.

activity.prompt: Usually part of CTC but NOT paid to you every month?
buckets: In CTC but not monthly in-hand

quiz.why: CTC (cost to company) includes employer PF and a gratuity provision, not just what you receive in hand.
In-hand salary is gross pay minus deductions such as PF, professional tax and TDS.
Variable pay usually depends on performance and is not guaranteed.

options: A state tax deducted from salary
quiz.why: Professional tax is a state tax deducted from salary. It is levied by states, up to ₹2,500 a year.
For monthly planning use the expected in-hand fixed pay, which is reliable cash. CTC ÷ 12 or bonuses overstate it.

scenes.text: Arjun notices his basic is only 40% of his fixed pay and asks why.
HR explains how basic affects PF, HRA and gratuity.

steps.title: Earnings
steps.body:
- **Basic:** foundation of salary; PF, gratuity and HRA exemption are calculated on it. Often 40–50% of fixed pay.
- **HRA (house rent allowance):** helps with rent; partly tax-exempt only under the **old** regime if you pay rent.
- **Special/flexi allowance:** balancing figure; fully taxable.
- **LTA (leave travel allowance):** old-regime exemption for domestic travel, within rules.
- **Bonus/variable, overtime, shift allowance.**
- **Reimbursements:** phone/internet/fuel against bills (taxability depends on rules/regime).

steps.title: Deductions
steps.body:
- **Employee PF:** 12% of basic (+DA). Many employers cap PF wages at ₹15,000/month, giving ₹1,800; others use full basic.
- **Professional tax:** state-level; max ₹2,500/year (some states don't levy it).
- **TDS:** income tax estimated for the year and deducted monthly.
- **ESI:** for employees earning up to ₹21,000/month gross — employee 0.75%, employer 3.25%.
- Others: voluntary PF, loan recovery, canteen, NPS.

steps.title: Solved example: effect of higher basic
steps.body:
Fixed ₹1,00,000/month. Basic 40% = ₹40,000 → employee PF ₹4,800 (uncapped). Basic 50% = ₹50,000 → PF ₹6,000.
**Effect:** higher basic → more forced savings (PF) and higher gratuity, but lower in-hand now.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking HRA is always tax-free — the exemption is old-regime only and needs actual rent.
- Not submitting rent receipts/landlord PAN (if rent > ₹1 lakh/year) when using the old regime.

activity.prompt: Match the component to its description.
pairs: Base for PF, gratuity and HRA exemption
Rent allowance; exemption only in old regime
Income tax deducted monthly by employer

quiz.why: PF is calculated on basic pay (plus DA), the PF wages, not on CTC or gross.
Professional tax is capped at ₹2,500 per year.
HRA exemption is available only under the old tax regime. The new regime removes it.
Special allowance is fully taxable. Unlike HRA, it carries no exemption.
A higher basic means higher PF and gratuity, since both are linked to basic pay.

lessons.title: Reading a payslip line by line

scenes.text: Meera's first payslip arrives as a PDF full of abbreviations.
She learns to check it in five minutes every month.

steps.title: Solved example: a monthly payslip
steps.body:
**Earnings:** Basic ₹35,000 · HRA ₹14,000 · Special allowance ₹21,000 · **Gross ₹70,000**
**Deductions:** Employee PF ₹4,200 · Professional tax ₹200 · TDS ₹3,600 · **Total ₹8,000**
**Net pay = 70,000 − 8,000 = ₹62,000**
Also shown: days paid, LOP (loss of pay) days, UAN, PAN, bank account, year-to-date totals.

steps.title: Monthly 5-point check
steps.body:
1) Days paid and LOP correct?
2) Gross matches offer?
3) PF = 12% of PF wages?
4) TDS reasonable for your declared regime?
5) Net = amount credited to bank?

steps.title: Identifiers
steps.body: **UAN** (Universal Account Number) is your lifelong PF number — keep it when you switch jobs. **PAN** links salary to your tax records; missing PAN can mean higher TDS.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not checking LOP — unapproved leave reduces pay.
- Not checking PF deposits in the EPFO passbook.
- Ignoring year-to-date TDS until March.

activity.prompt: Gross ₹82,000; PF ₹5,400; professional tax ₹200; TDS ₹6,400. Net pay?

quiz.why: LOP means loss of pay days, the unpaid days deducted from salary.
The UAN is your PF account number that stays the same across jobs. It is the EPFO identifier.
Net pay is gross pay minus deductions.
Check PF deposits in the EPFO member passbook.
Employee PF is 12% of basic: 12% × ₹30,000 = ₹3,600.

scenes.text: Kabir has two offers: ₹18 lakh CTC with 25% variable, and ₹16 lakh with 5% variable plus better insurance.
He compares fixed cash, benefits and risks — not just headline CTC.

steps.title: Solved example: fixed-cash comparison
steps.body:
**Offer A:** ₹18 L CTC, 25% variable (₹4.5 L), employer PF+gratuity ≈ ₹0.8 L → fixed ≈ ₹12.7 L.
**Offer B:** ₹16 L CTC, 5% variable (₹0.8 L), PF+gratuity ≈ ₹0.8 L → fixed ≈ ₹14.4 L.
**Insight:** B pays ₹1.7 L more guaranteed cash per year. A only wins if variable is reliably paid near 100%.

steps.title: Other factors
steps.body: Health insurance (cover amount, parents included?), term life cover, ESOPs/RSUs (vesting schedule, liquidity), joining bonus clawback, relocation, notice period, work location costs (rent), growth and learning, manager quality, job stability.

steps.title: Negotiation tip
steps.body: Negotiate on **fixed pay** first; ask for a joining bonus to cover a lost bonus at your current job; get changes in the revised offer letter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing CTC only.
- Valuing unvested startup ESOPs as cash.
- Ignoring long notice periods and clawback clauses.

activity.prompt: Offer comparison checklist
items: Variable % and last year's payout history
Employer PF and gratuity inside CTC?
Health insurance amount and family cover

quiz.q: Most reliable figure to compare offers:
quiz.why: Compare offers by fixed pay, the guaranteed part. Headline CTC, target bonus and ESOP paper value are uncertain.

options: You repay it if you leave early
quiz.why: A joining bonus clawback means you must repay it if you leave early, per the conditions.

quiz.q: Unvested ESOPs should be treated as:
quiz.why: Unvested ESOPs are uncertain future value, not cash or salary today.

quiz.q: Offer A fixed ₹12.7 L vs B ₹14.4 L: B gives more guaranteed cash by:
quiz.why: The difference in guaranteed cash is ₹14.4 L − ₹12.7 L = ₹1.7 L.
Negotiate fixed pay first, since it is the biggest and compounds into raises and benefits.

questions.q: CTC stands for:
questions.why: CTC stands for cost to company.

questions.q: In-hand salary is:
questions.why: In-hand salary is gross minus deductions, which is net pay.

questions.q: Employee PF rate:
questions.why: Employee PF is 12% of basic (plus DA), the statutory rate.

questions.q: Professional tax is levied by:
questions.why: Professional tax is levied by states, not the centre or employers.

questions.q: HRA exemption needs:
options: Old regime and actual rent paid
questions.why: HRA exemption needs the old regime and actual rent paid.

questions.q: ESI applies to employees with gross wages up to:
questions.why: ESI applies to employees with gross wages up to ₹21,000 per month.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Higher basic increases PF deductions. Reason (R): PF is a percentage of basic (+DA).
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: PF is a percentage of basic (plus DA), so a higher basic increases PF deductions.

questions.q: Which is usually in CTC but not in monthly in-hand?
questions.why: Employer PF is part of CTC but goes to your PF account, so it isn't in monthly in-hand pay.

questions.q: Which identifier stays the same across jobs for PF?
questions.why: The UAN stays the same across jobs for PF. Employee ID and payslip numbers change.

questions.q: Case: ₹20 L CTC, 30% variable, PF+gratuity ₹1 L. Fixed pay?
questions.why: Variable is 30% of ₹20 L = ₹6 L, and PF plus gratuity is ₹1 L, so fixed pay = 20 − 6 − 1 = ₹13 L.

questions.q: Case: Payslip shows 2 LOP days you didn't take. Best action?
options: Raise with HR/payroll with leave records
questions.why: Raise 2 incorrect LOP days promptly with HR or payroll, bringing your leave records. Waiting or ignoring it loses pay.

questions.q: Case: Two offers — A ₹15 L (fixed ₹13 L), B ₹14 L (fixed ₹13.5 L, better health cover). Purely on guaranteed value, which is better?
questions.why: On guaranteed value, B is better: ₹13.5 L fixed versus ₹13 L, plus better health cover. A's higher CTC is mostly variable.

questions.q: Why does a long notice period matter in offer comparison?
options: It can delay future switches and affect buyout costs
questions.why: A long notice period can delay future switches and affect buyout costs, so it matters when comparing offers.

questions.q: Basic ₹50,000/month, employer caps PF wages at ₹15,000. Employee PF/month?
questions.why: With PF wages capped at ₹15,000, employee PF = 12% × 15,000 = ₹1,800 a month.

courses.title: Ch 2 · PF, NPS, gratuity and insurance
courses.summary: How EPF and EPS contributions split, interest and withdrawals, VPF, PPF and NPS, the gratuity formula, and how to think about employer and personal insurance.
outcomes: Learners can compute employer EPF/EPS split
