Learners can compare VPF, PPF and NPS
Learners can calculate gratuity
Learners can choose adequate term and health insurance

scenes.text: Sana sees ₹3,600 employee PF but only ₹2,350 employer share in her EPF passbook.
The rest went to the pension scheme.

steps.title: How contributions split
steps.body:
- **Employee:** 12% of basic (+DA) → all to **EPF**.
- **Employer:** 12% of basic (+DA) → **8.33% to EPS** (Employees' Pension Scheme), calculated on wages capped at **₹15,000/month** (so max **₹1,250/month**), and the **balance to EPF**.

steps.title: Interest and tax
steps.body: EPF interest is declared yearly (8.25% for FY 2024-25). Interest is generally tax-free, but interest on **employee contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year** is taxable. Withdrawing before **5 years of continuous service** can make the withdrawal taxable (TDS may apply). EPS pension needs at least **10 years** of service; it's paid from age 58.

steps.title: Switching jobs
steps.body: Keep the same **UAN**; **transfer** old PF to the new account rather than withdrawing — it keeps compounding and preserves continuous service for tax purposes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Withdrawing PF at every job change.
- Not linking Aadhaar/PAN/bank to UAN (KYC).
- Forgetting to check that the employer is actually depositing.

activity.prompt: Basic ₹40,000. Employer's EPF share (after EPS of ₹1,250)?

quiz.q: Max employer EPS contribution per month:
quiz.why: The maximum employer EPS contribution is 8.33% of ₹15,000 = ₹1,250 a month.
EPF interest declared for FY 2024-25 is 8.25%.
EPS pension requires at least 10 years of service.

quiz.q: On job change, best is to:
options: Transfer PF under the same UAN
quiz.why: On a job change, transfer your PF under the same UAN. This keeps continuity and compounding.

quiz.q: Withdrawal before 5 years of continuous service may be:
quiz.why: Withdrawal before 5 years of continuous service may be taxable, so it is better to transfer.

scenes.text: Dev wants safe long-term savings and hears 'VPF, PPF, NPS' from colleagues.
He lines them up side by side.

steps.title: VPF (Voluntary PF)
steps.body: Extra contribution to your EPF beyond 12% (up to 100% of basic+DA), at the EPF rate. Employer doesn't match. Same tax treatment as EPF (watch the ₹2.5 lakh interest-taxable limit).

steps.title: PPF (Public Provident Fund)
steps.body: Government small-savings scheme at post offices/banks. **15-year** lock-in (extendable in 5-year blocks), deposit **₹500 to ₹1.5 lakh per year**, interest rate set by government quarterly (7.1% p.a. in recent quarters — check current). Interest and maturity are tax-free; deposits qualify for 80C under the old regime.

steps.title: NPS (National Pension System)
steps.body: Market-linked retirement scheme regulated by PFRDA. **Tier I** (locked till 60, with limited partial withdrawals) and **Tier II** (flexible). At 60, up to **60%** can be withdrawn tax-free; at least **40%** must buy an annuity (pension). Tax: employer contribution deductible under section 80CCD(2) (up to 14% of basic+DA in the new regime; 10% in old for private employees); extra ₹50,000 under 80CCD(1B) in the old regime.

steps.title: Solved example: pick for a goal
steps.body:
- Safe, tax-free, long-term, flexible amount → **PPF**.
- Already in EPF, want more guaranteed-rate savings via payroll → **VPF**.
- Retirement with equity exposure and employer NPS benefit in the new regime → **NPS (corporate)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Locking emergency money in PPF/NPS.
- Ignoring that NPS returns are market-linked, not guaranteed.

This is general education, not financial or tax advice; limits and rates change — verify current rules.

activity.prompt: Match the feature.

quiz.why: PPF has a 15-year lock-in.
The maximum PPF deposit is ₹1.5 lakh per year.
At 60, at least 40% of the NPS corpus must go to an annuity.

quiz.q: Employer NPS deduction in new regime is up to:
quiz.why: Under the new regime, employer NPS contribution is deductible up to 14% of basic plus DA, under Section 80CCD(2).
NPS returns are market-linked, since the corpus is invested in markets. They aren't guaranteed.

scenes.text: Vikram resigns after 6 years and 8 months. Last basic: ₹52,000.
HR calculates his gratuity — and he checks it himself.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body:
Under the **Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972**, an employee who has rendered **at least 5 years of continuous service** gets gratuity on leaving (the 5-year condition doesn't apply on death or disablement). Formula for covered employees:
**Gratuity = 15 × last drawn (basic + DA) × completed years ÷ 26**
A part-year of **more than 6 months** counts as a full year. The statutory ceiling is **₹20 lakh**, and tax exemption for private employees is up to ₹20 lakh.

steps.title: Labour Codes
steps.body: India's four Labour Codes, including the **Code on Social Security, 2020**, have been brought into force, and they change some rules — for example, **fixed-term employees** become eligible for gratuity after **one year**, and a wider definition of 'wages' can increase PF and gratuity amounts. Rules are being phased in; check your employer's policy and the latest notifications.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gross salary instead of basic+DA.
- Forgetting the 6-month rounding rule.
- Assuming gratuity in CTC means you get it if you leave in year 2 (as a permanent employee, generally not).

activity.prompt: Last basic ₹39,000, service 10 years 3 months (counts as 10 years). Gratuity?

quiz.why: The gratuity formula is 15/26 of last drawn salary per year of service, so the divisor is 26.
For gratuity, a service period of more than 6 months in the last year rounds up, so 5 years 7 months counts as 6 years.
Gratuity uses last drawn basic plus DA, not gross or CTC.

quiz.q: Tax-exempt gratuity limit for private employees:
quiz.why: The tax-exempt gratuity limit for private employees is ₹20 lakh.

lessons.title: Insurance: employer cover vs your own

scenes.text: Neel quits to start a business. Two months later he's hospitalised.
His company health cover ended on his last day.

steps.title: Group cover
steps.body: Employers often give group health insurance (sometimes covering spouse, children, parents) and group term life. **It ends when you leave.** Keep a **personal** health policy too, ideally bought young (lower premiums, waiting periods finished).

steps.title: Term life insurance
steps.body: Pure protection: pays the nominee if you die during the term; no maturity value; cheapest per rupee of cover. Common rule of thumb: cover of **10–15× annual income** plus outstanding loans, if others depend on you.

steps.title: Health insurance basics
steps.body: Sum insured, room-rent limits, co-pay, waiting periods for pre-existing diseases, network hospitals, cashless vs reimbursement, top-up/super top-up policies to increase cover cheaply.

steps.title: Solved example: how much term cover?
steps.body:
Income ₹12 lakh/year, home loan ₹30 lakh, two dependants.
**Step 1:** 12 × 12 lakh ≈ ₹1.44 crore.
**Step 2:** + loan ₹30 lakh → ≈ ₹1.7 crore → choose ₹1.75 crore term cover till age 60.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Buying endowment/money-back plans as 'investment + insurance' — usually low returns and low cover.
- Relying only on employer cover.
- Hiding medical history — claims can be rejected.

This is general education, not financial advice.

Term insurance pays only if death occurs during the term.
A super top-up can raise health cover cheaply above a deductible.
Mixing insurance and investment usually gives the best of both.
statements.why: Typically low cover and low returns.

Group health cover usually ends when you leave the job, since it is tied to employment.
Waiting periods apply to pre-existing diseases under health policy terms.
Term insurance is pure risk cover, so it has no maturity value.

quiz.why: Hiding medical history is non-disclosure and can lead to claim rejection.

questions.q: PPF lock-in:
questions.why: PPF has a 15-year lock-in.

questions.q: Gratuity minimum service (normal case):
questions.why: Gratuity normally needs a minimum of 5 years of continuous service, per the Act.

questions.q: Term insurance is:
questions.why: Term insurance is pure life cover, giving protection with no savings component.

questions.q: NPS regulator:
questions.why: The NPS regulator is PFRDA. SEBI regulates markets, IRDAI insurance and RBI banks.

questions.q: EPF interest FY 2024-25:
questions.why: The EPF interest rate declared for FY 2024-25 is 8.25%.

questions.q: Basic ₹25,000: monthly total into EPF (employee + employer EPF part)?
questions.why: Employee EPF is 12% of ₹25,000 = ₹3,000. The employer's 12% is ₹3,000, of which ₹1,250 goes to EPS, leaving ₹1,750 for EPF. So EPF = 3,000 + 1,750 = ₹4,750.

questions.q: Gratuity: basic ₹65,000, 8 years 7 months?
questions.why: 8 years 7 months rounds up to 9 years, so gratuity = 15 × ₹65,000 × 9 ÷ 26 = ₹3,37,500.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Withdrawing PF at every switch hurts wealth. Reason (R): It breaks compounding and may make withdrawals taxable.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: withdrawing PF at every switch breaks compounding and may make withdrawals taxable.

questions.q: NPS lump sum at 60 tax-free up to:
questions.why: The NPS lump sum at 60 is tax-free up to 60% of the corpus, with the remaining 40% going to an annuity.

questions.q: Case: You're 27, single, no dependants, no loans. Term insurance priority?
options: Lower now; health insurance first; buy term when dependants/loans arrive (or early for low premium)
questions.why: At 27 with no dependants or loans, term cover can be lower now. Take health insurance first and buy term when dependants or loans arrive, or early for a low premium.

questions.q: Case: Employee contributes ₹3.5 lakh/year to EPF+VPF. Tax issue?
options: Interest on contributions above ₹2.5 lakh is taxable
questions.why: Contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year to EPF and VPF make the interest on the excess taxable. The contribution itself isn't illegal.

questions.q: Case: A permanent employee resigns after 4 years 3 months (no death or disablement). Under the 1972 Act's rule, gratuity is:
options: Generally not payable — less than 5 years of continuous service
questions.why: Gratuity needs 5 years of continuous service, apart from death or disablement. At 4 years 3 months it is generally not payable.

questions.q: Income ₹15 L, loans ₹40 L, dependants. Rule-of-thumb term cover?
questions.why: 10 to 15 times ₹15 L is ₹1.5–2.25 crore, and adding the ₹40 L loans gives about ₹1.9–2.65 crore.

questions.q: Why prefer transferring PF to withdrawing when switching jobs?
options: Preserves continuous service for tax and keeps compounding
questions.why: Transferring PF preserves continuous service for tax purposes and keeps compounding. Withdrawing breaks both.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Income tax for salaried employees: old vs new regime
courses.summary: Tax basics (financial year, TDS, Form 16, AIS), the new regime slabs and rebate with worked examples, the old regime with deductions, choosing a regime and filing your return. Figures are for FY 2025-26 as announced in Budget 2025; verify the current year.
outcomes: Learners can explain FY, TDS, Form 16, Form 26AS/AIS and the ITR deadline
Learners can compute tax under the new regime
Learners can compute tax under the old regime with common deductions
Learners can choose a regime and avoid common filing mistakes

lessons.title: Tax basics: year, TDS, Form 16, AIS

scenes.text: In June, HR emails Pooja her Form 16. She has no idea what to do with it.
Her friend shows her the income-tax portal, AIS and how to file.

steps.title: The year
steps.body: Income is taxed for a **financial year** (1 April – 31 March). Under the Income-tax Act, 1961 you filed in the following 'assessment year'. The new **Income-tax Act, 2025** applies from **1 April 2026** and uses the simpler term **'tax year'**; section numbers change too (e.g. what you know as '80C' is renumbered). Concepts in this course still apply — check updated names in the forms.

steps.title: TDS and documents
steps.body:
- **TDS:** employer estimates your annual tax and deducts it monthly.
- **Form 16:** employer's certificate of salary paid and TDS deducted (issued by mid-June).
- **Form 26AS / AIS / TIS:** tax department's statements of TDS and other income (interest, dividends, securities trades) reported about you.
- **ITR:** your return. Due date for most salaried individuals (no audit): **31 July** after the year ends.

steps.title: Solved example: reconcile before filing
steps.body:
Form 16 TDS: ₹84,000. AIS shows TDS ₹84,000 ✔, plus savings interest ₹12,500 and FD interest ₹30,000 not in Form 16.
**Action:** include the interest under 'income from other sources' in the ITR; pay any extra tax before filing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking TDS means no return is needed.
- Ignoring interest income shown in AIS → notices.
- Missing 31 July → late fee and loss of some benefits.

This is general education, not tax advice.

activity.prompt: Match the term.
pairs: Department's statement of your reported income
Term used by the Income-tax Act, 2025

quiz.why: India's financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March.
Form 16 is issued by your employer, showing your salary and TDS.

quiz.q: Interest income appearing in AIS should be:
quiz.why: Interest income that appears in AIS is taxable, so report it in your ITR.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026.

quiz.q: Usual ITR due date for salaried (no audit):
quiz.why: The usual ITR due date for salaried employees without audit is 31 July.

scenes.text: Rahul hears 'no tax up to ₹12 lakh' and wonders how his ₹12.75 lakh salary pays zero.
Standard deduction and the rebate explain it.

steps.title: Slabs (FY 2025-26)
steps.body:
New regime (default under section 115BAC):
- Up to ₹4,00,000: nil
- ₹4–8 lakh: 5%
- ₹8–12 lakh: 10%
- ₹12–16 lakh: 15%
- ₹16–20 lakh: 20%
- ₹20–24 lakh: 25%
- Above ₹24 lakh: 30%
Plus **4% health & education cess** on tax (and surcharge at high incomes).

steps.title: Standard deduction and rebate
steps.body:
- **Standard deduction:** ₹75,000 for salaried in the new regime.
- **Section 87A rebate:** if taxable income ≤ **₹12,00,000**, rebate up to **₹60,000** → tax becomes nil (marginal relief applies just above ₹12 lakh). The rebate doesn't apply to special-rate income like capital gains.
- Most old deductions (80C, 80D, HRA) are **not** allowed; employer NPS under 80CCD(2) **is** allowed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting standard deduction.
- Applying 30% to the whole income instead of slab-by-slab.
- Forgetting the 4% cess.

Slabs can change every Budget — check the current year's numbers.

activity.prompt: New regime, salary ₹15,00,000. Total tax including 4% cess? (taxable = ₹14,25,000)

quiz.why: The new-regime standard deduction for FY 2025-26 is ₹75,000.

quiz.q: 87A rebate makes tax nil if taxable income is up to:
quiz.why: The 87A rebate makes tax nil if taxable income is up to ₹12 lakh in FY 2025-26 under the new regime.
In the new regime, income between ₹8 and ₹12 lakh is taxed at 10%.
Health and education cess is 4% of the tax.

quiz.q: Which deduction is allowed in the new regime?
quiz.why: Employer NPS contribution under Section 80CCD(2) is allowed in the new regime. 80C, 80D and HRA exemption are not.

scenes.text: Anita pays ₹25,000 rent, invests ₹1.5 lakh in PPF/ELSS and buys health insurance.
She checks whether the old regime saves her money.

steps.title: Old regime slabs (individuals below 60)
steps.body:
- Up to ₹2,50,000: nil
- ₹2.5–5 lakh: 5%
- ₹5–10 lakh: 20%
- Above ₹10 lakh: 30%
+ 4% cess. **87A rebate** up to ₹12,500 if taxable income ≤ ₹5 lakh. **Standard deduction ₹50,000** for salaried.

steps.title: Common deductions/exemptions
steps.body:
- **80C:** up to ₹1,50,000 (EPF, PPF, ELSS, life premium, principal of home loan, tuition fees, 5-year tax-saver FD)
- **80CCD(1B):** extra ₹50,000 for own NPS
- **80D:** health insurance — ₹25,000 for self/family (+ up to ₹25,000, or ₹50,000 if parents are senior citizens)
- **HRA exemption:** least of (actual HRA; rent − 10% of basic; 50% of basic in metros/40% elsewhere)
- **Section 24(b):** home-loan interest up to ₹2,00,000 for self-occupied property

steps.title: Solved example: salary ₹15 lakh, old regime
steps.body:
Deductions: standard 50,000; 80C 1,50,000; 80D 25,000; HRA exempt 2,00,000; 80CCD(1B) 50,000 → total 4,75,000.
Taxable = 15,00,000 − 4,75,000 = **10,25,000**.
Tax: 2.5–5 L = 12,500; 5–10 L = 1,00,000; 10–10.25 L = 7,500 → 1,20,000; cess 4,800 → **₹1,24,800**.
**New regime** for the same salary: **₹97,500** (see previous lesson). → New regime is cheaper here despite ₹4.75 L of deductions.

steps.title: Solved example: HRA exemption
steps.body:
Basic ₹40,000/month (₹4.8 L/yr), HRA ₹20,000/month (₹2.4 L/yr), rent ₹25,000/month (₹3 L/yr), metro.
(a) Actual HRA = 2,40,000
(b) Rent − 10% basic = 3,00,000 − 48,000 = 2,52,000
(c) 50% of basic = 2,40,000
**Exempt = least = ₹2,40,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Investing in poor products just for 80C.
- Claiming HRA while living in own house without paying rent.
- Assuming the old regime is always better because you have deductions — calculate both.

activity.prompt: Old regime: taxable income ₹8,00,000 (below 60). Tax including 4% cess?

quiz.why: The 80C deduction limit is ₹1,50,000.
The old-regime standard deduction is ₹50,000.
Home-loan interest on a self-occupied property can be deducted up to ₹2,00,000 under Section 24(b).
In the old regime, income above ₹10 lakh is taxed at 30%.
HRA exemption is the least of three amounts, so you get the smallest one.

lessons.title: Choosing a regime and filing well

scenes.text: In April, HR asks Karthik to choose a regime for TDS.
He runs both calculations instead of guessing.

steps.title: How to choose
steps.body:
1) Compute tax in the **new** regime (standard deduction only, plus employer NPS).
2) Compute tax in the **old** regime with deductions you **actually** have.
3) Pick the lower. Rough guide (FY 2025-26): with the higher new-regime rebate and slabs, many salaried people pay less under the new regime unless they have large deductions (big HRA + home-loan interest + full 80C/80D/NPS).

steps.title: Switching
steps.body: Salaried individuals (without business income) can choose the regime **each year** when filing the return, even if they told the employer differently for TDS. Those with business income have restrictions on switching back and forth.

steps.title: Solved example: break-even thinking
steps.body: Salary ₹15 L: new-regime tax ₹97,500 (₹93,750 before cess). To beat it, old-regime tax before cess must fall below ₹93,750: 12,500 + 20% × (T − 5,00,000) < 93,750 → **T < ₹9,06,250**. So old-regime taxable income must be about ₹9.06 lakh or less → deductions of about **₹5.94 lakh or more** (including the ₹50,000 standard deduction). Without large rent and home-loan interest that's hard.

steps.title: Filing checklist
steps.body: Download AIS/26AS → match Form 16 → add interest, dividends, capital gains → choose regime → pay any balance tax → file ITR before 31 July → **e-verify** within the allowed time (Aadhaar OTP/net banking) → track refund.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Filing but not e-verifying (the return isn't complete).
- Wrong bank account for refund (must be pre-validated).
- Ignoring capital gains from mutual fund redemptions.

This is general education, not tax advice. Rules and numbers change with each Budget and the new Act — verify for the current year.

activity.prompt: Order the filing steps.
items: Compute tax in both regimes and choose
File the ITR before the due date

quiz.q: A return is complete only after:
quiz.why: A return is complete only after e-verification. Without it, the return is treated as not filed.

quiz.q: Salaried individuals without business income can choose the regime:
quiz.why: Salaried individuals without business income can choose their regime each year at filing.

quiz.q: Best way to choose a regime:
quiz.why: Choose a regime by calculating both with your real numbers, as the better one is personal.

quiz.q: Capital gains on fund redemption should be:
quiz.why: Capital gains on fund redemption are taxable income and should be reported.
The refund goes to a pre-validated bank account.

questions.q: Default regime for FY 2025-26:
questions.why: The new regime is the default for FY 2025-26 under Section 115BAC. You must opt out to choose the old one.

questions.q: Cess on income tax:
questions.why: Cess on income tax is 4%, as health and education cess.

questions.q: Form 16 shows:
questions.why: Form 16 shows your salary and the TDS deducted by your employer.

questions.q: New-regime nil slab (FY 2025-26):
questions.why: The new-regime nil slab for FY 2025-26 is up to ₹4 lakh.

questions.q: 80D covers:
questions.why: Section 80D covers health insurance premiums.

questions.q: HRA exemption exists in:
questions.why: HRA exemption exists only in the old regime.

questions.q: New regime, salary ₹12,75,000 → tax:
questions.why: ₹12,75,000 minus the ₹75,000 standard deduction is ₹12 lakh taxable, which the 87A rebate makes nil.

questions.q: Old regime taxable ₹10,00,000 → tax incl. cess:
Assertion (A): TDS deducted means no ITR needed. Reason (R): Other income like FD interest may be taxable.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: other income like FD interest may be taxable, so TDS alone doesn't remove the need to file or report.

questions.q: HRA: actual HRA ₹1.8 L, rent − 10% basic ₹2.1 L, 40% of basic ₹1.6 L. Exempt?
questions.why: HRA exemption is the least of the three amounts: ₹1.6 L (40% of basic) is the smallest of ₹1.8 L, ₹2.1 L and ₹1.6 L.

questions.q: New regime, salary ₹25,75,000 → taxable ₹25 L. Tax before cess?
Case: Salary ₹10 L, no rent, no home loan, 80C ₹1.5 L. Which regime is likely cheaper?
questions.why: Salary ₹10 L less the ₹75,000 standard deduction is ₹9.25 L, which is below ₹12 L, so the new regime gives nil tax after rebate. The old regime would still tax it.

questions.q: Case: You told HR 'new regime' but have big rent and home-loan interest. Can you choose old when filing (salaried, no business income)?
questions.why: Yes. Salaried people with no business income can choose the old regime when filing, even if HR assumed the new one.

questions.q: Case: New regime salary ₹20,75,000 (taxable ₹20 L). Tax with cess?
Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, which statement is right?
options: It applies from 1 April 2026 and uses 'tax year'; section numbers change
questions.why: The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026, uses 'tax year' and changes section numbers. It doesn't abolish income tax or TDS.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Budgeting, emergency fund, credit and loans
courses.summary: Simple budgets that work, building an emergency fund, credit cards and credit scores, and understanding EMIs and loans.
outcomes: Learners can build a 50/30/20-style budget and automate savings
Learners can size and place an emergency fund
Learners can use credit cards without interest and protect their credit score
Learners can calculate an EMI and the true cost of a loan

scenes.text: Every month Aditya's salary vanishes by the 20th — food delivery, weekend trips, gadgets.
He tries 'pay yourself first' with three buckets.

steps.title: 50/30/20 as a starting point
steps.body: Of take-home pay: **50% needs** (rent, groceries, EMIs, utilities, insurance), **30% wants** (eating out, travel, shopping), **20% savings & investing**. Adjust to your city and stage — freshers in metros may need 60/20/20; aim to raise savings with each raise.

steps.title: Pay yourself first
steps.body: On salary day, auto-transfer savings (SIP, RD, emergency fund) **before** spending. Spend what remains guilt-free.

steps.title: Solved example: ₹60,000 take-home
steps.body:
Needs 50% = ₹30,000 (rent ₹15,000, food ₹8,000, utilities ₹2,000, transport ₹3,000, insurance ₹2,000)
Wants 30% = ₹18,000
Savings 20% = ₹12,000 → ₹5,000 emergency fund + ₹7,000 SIP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Tracking but not automating.
- 'Lifestyle creep' — spending every raise.
- Forgetting annual costs (insurance, festivals) — divide by 12 and save monthly.

activity.label: Share of take-home pay you save each month

bands.text: Very low — start with an automatic ₹1,000–2,000 transfer on salary day.
A start — try to reach 20% as income grows.
Excellent — make sure essentials and insurance are covered too.

quiz.why: In the 50/30/20 rule, 50% is for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings and investing.
'Pay yourself first' means saving automatically before you spend.
Lifestyle creep is spending that rises with every raise, so savings don't grow.

quiz.q: Annual insurance premium ₹12,000 → monthly saving needed:
quiz.why: An annual premium of ₹12,000 needs ₹12,000 ÷ 12 = ₹1,000 saved each month.
Rent and groceries are needs, the essentials.

scenes.text: Tanya's company cuts 15% of staff. She's one of them.
Her six-month emergency fund gives her time to find the right next job.

steps.title: How much
steps.body: Typically **3–6 months of essential expenses** (more — 6 to 12 months — if income is variable, you're the sole earner, or you work in a volatile industry). Build it before investing in risky assets.

steps.title: Where to keep it
steps.body: Safe and accessible: savings account, sweep-in FD, short FDs, or liquid/overnight mutual funds. **Not** in equities, PPF or NPS.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Essential expenses ₹35,000/month; sole earner → target 6 months = **₹2,10,000**. Saving ₹10,000/month → reached in 21 months; speed up with part of bonus.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the emergency fund for a holiday.
- Keeping it in volatile investments.
- Counting a credit card limit as an emergency fund.

activity.prompt: Essential expenses ₹28,000/month; target 6 months. Emergency fund needed?

quiz.why: A typical emergency fund is 3 to 6 months of expenses.
Keep an emergency fund in a sweep FD or liquid fund, which is safe and easy to withdraw. Crypto, small-caps and PPF are volatile or locked.
Build the emergency fund before risky investing, as it is the foundation.
A credit card limit is debt, not an emergency fund.
Sole earners carry more risk, so they should aim for a higher fund of 6 to 12 months.

scenes.text: Rohan pays only the 'minimum due' of ₹2,500 on a ₹50,000 bill.
Next month, interest of over ₹1,500 appears — and his free credit period is gone.

steps.title: How card interest works
steps.body: Pay the **full statement balance** by the due date → no interest (interest-free period). Pay less → interest (often around 3–3.75% per month, i.e. roughly 36–45% a year) on the outstanding amount, and new purchases may also attract interest until fully cleared. Cash withdrawals attract interest from day one plus fees.

steps.title: Credit scores
steps.body: Credit bureaus in India (e.g. TransUnion CIBIL, Experian, Equifax, CRIF High Mark) give scores typically **300–900**; above ~750 is generally considered good. Drivers: **on-time payments**, **credit utilisation** (keep under ~30% of limit), credit mix, age of accounts, and number of recent loan/card applications.

steps.title: Solved example: utilisation
steps.body:
Limit ₹1,00,000; monthly spend ₹45,000 → utilisation 45% (high).
Option: keep spend ~₹30,000, or request a higher limit (and don't spend more), or pay mid-cycle before the statement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paying only minimum due.
- Converting everything into EMIs with processing fees.
- Many card/loan applications at once.
- Missing one payment — late fees and score drop.

statements.s: Paying the full statement balance by the due date avoids interest.
Paying the minimum due avoids all interest.
Keeping utilisation under ~30% helps your score.
Cash withdrawals on a credit card are interest-free for 45 days.

quiz.why: Indian credit scores typically range from 300 to 900.
On-time payments are the biggest factor in a credit score, since payment history carries the most weight.
A utilisation of 60% is high and risky for your score. Aim to stay under 30%.
3.5% a month is about 3.5 × 12 = 42% per year (simple).
Paying only the minimum due leaves interest on the remaining balance, which is the trap.

lessons.title: Loans and EMIs

scenes.text: Nisha wants a ₹10 lakh car loan at 9% for 5 years.
She calculates the EMI and total interest before signing.

steps.title: EMI formula
steps.body:
**EMI = P × r × (1+r)ⁿ ÷ [(1+r)ⁿ − 1]**
P = principal, r = monthly rate (annual ÷ 12 ÷ 100), n = number of months.
Early EMIs are mostly interest; later EMIs are mostly principal.

steps.title: Good vs costly debt
steps.body: Home loans and education loans can build assets/skills at lower rates; personal loans, credit card debt and 'buy now pay later' for wants are costly. Rule of thumb: keep total EMIs under ~30–40% of take-home pay.

steps.title: Prepayment
steps.body: Prepaying principal early saves the most interest. Floating-rate loans for individuals generally have no prepayment penalty under RBI rules; check your agreement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing only EMI, not total cost (longer tenure = lower EMI but more interest).
- Ignoring processing fees and insurance bundled with loans.
- Taking loans on instant-loan apps not regulated by RBI — check the lender is an RBI-regulated bank/NBFC.

activity.prompt: EMI ₹20,758 for 60 months on a ₹10,00,000 loan. Total interest paid (₹, nearest 100)?

quiz.q: In the EMI formula, r is:
quiz.why: In the EMI formula, r is the monthly interest rate, as a decimal.
A longer tenure gives a lower EMI but more total interest.
Early EMIs are mostly interest, due to amortisation, with the principal share growing later.
Keep total EMIs under about 30–40% of take-home pay to stay safe.

quiz.q: Before using a loan app, check:
quiz.why: Before using a loan app, check that the lender is RBI-regulated to avoid illegal lenders.

sources: RBI guidelines on loans and digital lending

questions.q: Emergency fund size:
questions.why: An emergency fund should be about 3 to 6 months of expenses.

questions.q: Pay full card balance by due date →
questions.why: Paying the full card balance by the due date means no interest is charged.
In 50/30/20, 50% goes to needs.

questions.q: Good credit score is generally above:
questions.why: A good credit score is generally above 750.

questions.q: Emergency fund should be in:
questions.why: An emergency fund should be in liquid, safe options so you can access it quickly. Equity and real estate can fall or be hard to sell.

questions.q: Credit utilisation target:
questions.why: Aim for credit utilisation under about 30%, which is healthy for your score.

questions.q: Take-home ₹80,000, 20% savings =
Assertion (A): Longer loan tenure reduces total interest. Reason (R): EMI falls with longer tenure.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: EMI falls with a longer tenure, but total interest rises.

questions.q: Monthly rate for 12% p.a.:
questions.why: 12% a year is 12 ÷ 12 = 1% a month, which is 0.01 as a decimal.

questions.q: Cash withdrawal on credit card:
questions.why: A cash withdrawal on a credit card charges interest from day one plus fees. It is costly.

questions.q: Case: ₹5 lakh loan, 12% p.a., 1 year: EMI ≈ ? ((1.01)¹² ≈ 1.1268)
Case: You owe ₹80,000 on a card at 3.5%/month and have ₹1 lakh in a savings account (beyond emergency fund). Best move?
questions.why: Pay off the card, since 3.5% a month costs about 42% a year. No investment reliably earns that, and minimum payments or a new card keep the debt growing.

questions.q: Case: Total EMIs ₹45,000 on take-home ₹90,000. Assessment?
options: 50% — too high; avoid new debt and plan prepayment
questions.why: EMIs of ₹45,000 on ₹90,000 take-home is 50%, above the safe 30–40%. That is too high, so avoid new debt and plan prepayment.

questions.q: Which reduces total interest most on a home loan?
questions.why: Prepaying principal early cuts the balance on which interest is charged, so it reduces total interest the most. Paying late, skipping EMIs or extending the tenure adds cost.

questions.q: Essential expenses ₹40,000, sole earner in volatile industry. Reasonable emergency fund?
questions.why: For a sole earner in a volatile industry, aim at the higher range of 6 to 12 months of essential expenses: 6 × ₹40,000 = ₹2.4 lakh to 12 × ₹40,000 = ₹4.8 lakh.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Investing basics
courses.summary: Inflation and compounding, the main investment options in India, mutual funds and SIPs, and risk, asset allocation, taxes on gains and how to avoid scams.
outcomes: Learners can use the Rule of 72 and compound-interest formula
Learners can compare FDs, PPF, debt funds, equity and gold
Learners can explain NAV, SIP, expense ratio, direct vs regular and index funds
Learners can build a simple asset allocation and spot investment scams

scenes.text: Grandma kept ₹1 lakh in cash in a locker for 10 years.
With 6% inflation, it buys what about ₹56,000 bought when she put it there.

steps.title: Inflation
steps.body: Prices rise over time. Purchasing power after n years ≈ amount ÷ (1 + inflation)ⁿ. At 6% for 10 years: 1 ÷ 1.06¹⁰ ≈ 0.558 → ₹1 lakh buys what ₹55,800 did. **Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation.**

steps.title: Solved example: start early
steps.body:
Asha invests ₹1 lakh at 25; Babu invests ₹1 lakh at 35. Both earn 10% until 60.
Asha: 1.1³⁵ ≈ 28.1 → ₹28.1 lakh. Babu: 1.1²⁵ ≈ 10.8 → ₹10.8 lakh.
**Ten extra years nearly tripled the result.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring inflation when calling something 'safe'.
- Waiting for the 'perfect time' to start.

activity.prompt: Rule of 72: years to double money at 9% a year?

quiz.why: By the Rule of 72, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years at 6%.
Real return is approximately the nominal return minus inflation.
₹1 lakh at 12% for 10 years grows to 1.12¹⁰ ≈ 3.106 times, so about ₹3.1 lakh.

quiz.q: Cash in a locker over 10 years at 6% inflation:
quiz.why: Cash in a locker earns nothing, so at 6% inflation it loses purchasing power over 10 years.
Starting early helps because of compounding over more years, as returns earn returns.

scenes.text: Karan's parents trust only FDs. His friends talk about stocks.
He maps each option by risk, return and liquidity.

steps.title: Main options
steps.body:
- **Savings account / FDs / RDs:** low risk, fixed returns, interest taxed at slab rate; bank deposits insured up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank by DICGC.
- **PPF, EPF, small savings:** government-backed, long lock-ins.
- **Debt mutual funds:** bonds/money-market; low-moderate risk; returns not guaranteed.
- **Equity (stocks, equity funds):** highest long-term growth potential, high short-term volatility; best for 5+ year goals.
- **Gold:** diversifier (gold ETFs/funds avoid making charges and storage risk).
- **Real estate:** large, illiquid, high transaction costs.

steps.title: Solved example: match goal to option
steps.body:
- Emergency fund → savings/sweep FD/liquid fund.
- Laptop in 1 year → FD/RD or short debt fund.
- House down-payment in 4 years → mostly debt + some equity.
- Retirement in 30 years → mostly equity (index funds) + EPF/PPF/NPS.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equity money needed next year.
- Judging funds by last year's return only.
- Treating insurance-cum-investment plans as investments.

activity.prompt: Best fit by time horizon.

items.text: FD/RD for a trip next year
PPF for a child's education in 15 years
Equity fund for a goal 20 years away

quiz.q: DICGC insures bank deposits up to:
quiz.why: DICGC insures bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
For a 20-year goal, diversified equity offers growth over the long term. FDs and savings accounts may lag inflation, and cash loses value.
FD interest is taxed at your slab rate, as other income.
Equity's main short-term risk is volatility, meaning price swings. It does have long-term growth potential.
Gold ETFs avoid making charges and storage risk, since gold is held in paper form. They still carry price risk and are taxed.

scenes.text: Leena starts a ₹5,000 monthly SIP in an index fund.
The market falls 15% in her first year. She keeps going — and buys more units cheaply.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **NAV:** price per unit of a fund.
- **SIP:** fixed amount invested regularly (e.g. monthly) — builds discipline and averages purchase cost (**rupee-cost averaging**).
- **Expense ratio:** annual fee as % of assets.
- **Direct vs regular plans:** direct plans have no distributor commission → lower expense ratio.
- **Index funds/ETFs:** track an index (e.g. Nifty 50) at low cost.
- **ELSS:** equity tax-saving funds with a 3-year lock-in (80C in the old regime).
- **Riskometer:** SEBI-mandated risk label on every scheme.

steps.title: Solved example: rupee-cost averaging
steps.body:
₹6,000 per month for 3 months at NAV ₹20, ₹15, ₹30.
Units = 300 + 400 + 200 = 900. Average cost = 18,000 ÷ 900 = **₹20** (lower than the average NAV of ₹21.67).

steps.title: Solved example: cost of fees
steps.body: ₹10 lakh for 20 years at 12% gross. Expense 0.2% → net 11.8% → ≈ ₹93.1 lakh. Expense 1.5% → net 10.5% → ≈ ₹73.7 lakh. **Fee difference ≈ ₹19 lakh.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping SIPs when markets fall (when units are cheapest).
- Owning 15 overlapping funds.
- Chasing last year's top performer.

Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks; read scheme documents.

activity.prompt: SIP of ₹5,000 each month at NAVs ₹25, ₹20, ₹50. Total units bought?

options: Price per unit of a fund
quiz.why: NAV is the net asset value, which is the price per unit of a fund.
Direct plans have a lower expense ratio because they carry no distributor commission. Returns aren't guaranteed.
ELSS funds have a 3-year lock-in, the shortest among 80C options.

options: More units when prices are low
quiz.why: Rupee-cost averaging invests a fixed amount regularly, so it buys more units when prices are low and fewer when prices are high.
Every mutual fund scheme carries a SEBI-mandated riskometer showing its risk level.

lessons.title: Risk, allocation, taxes on gains and scams

scenes.text: A Telegram group promises '5% a week guaranteed' on stock tips.
Sameer checks: no SEBI registration, guaranteed returns, pressure to pay fast. He leaves the group.

steps.title: Asset allocation
steps.body: Split money across equity, debt and gold based on **goal horizon** and **risk tolerance**. Example for a 28-year-old saving for retirement: 70% equity (mostly index funds), 25% debt (EPF/PPF/debt funds), 5% gold. **Rebalance** yearly back to targets. Diversify within asset classes.

steps.title: Tax on gains (from 23 July 2024)
steps.body:
- **Listed equity/equity funds:** short-term (≤12 months) gains taxed at **20%**; long-term (>12 months) gains above **₹1.25 lakh** a year taxed at **12.5%**.
- **Debt funds** bought on or after 1 April 2023: gains taxed at slab rates.
Rules change — verify current provisions.

steps.title: Scam red flags
steps.body: Guaranteed high returns · pressure to act now · tips via WhatsApp/Telegram · 'pay to join' trading groups · fake apps · requests to share demat login/OTP · unregistered advisers. Check SEBI registration of investment advisers/research analysts on SEBI's website; report fraud to **1930** / cybercrime.gov.in and to SEBI's SCORES.

steps.title: Solved example: LTCG tax
steps.body:
Sold equity fund units held 3 years with gain ₹2,00,000 in the year.
Exempt ₹1,25,000 → taxable ₹75,000 × 12.5% = **₹9,375** (+ cess).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- All money in one stock or sector.
- Panic-selling in a crash.
- Trading futures & options without understanding risk — SEBI studies have found most individual F&O traders lose money.

This is general education, not investment advice.

a.text: A stranger adds you to a group: 'Guaranteed 30% a month! Pay ₹10,000 joining fee.' What do you do?

choices.label: Pay — others are posting profits
choices.feedback: Screenshots of profits are easy to fake.

choices.label: Check SEBI registration, see 'guaranteed' red flag, leave and report

b.text: They ask for more money to 'unlock withdrawals'. What now?

choices.label: Stop paying; report to 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in

c.text: You avoided a classic investment scam. Real investments never guarantee such returns.

d.text: You may recover some money if reported quickly. Lesson: guarantees + urgency = scam.

quiz.q: LTCG on listed equity (from 23 July 2024) above ₹1.25 lakh:
quiz.why: From 23 July 2024, LTCG on listed equity above ₹1.25 lakh is taxed at 12.5%.
From 23 July 2024, short-term capital gains on listed equity are taxed at 20%.
Rebalancing means returning your portfolio to its target allocation, which keeps risk in check by selling what has grown and buying what lagged.
'Guaranteed 30% a month' is an impossible promise, so it is a scam red flag. No legitimate investment guarantees such returns.
Check advisers in SEBI's official registration database. WhatsApp, Instagram or reviews aren't reliable proof.

sources: Income-tax provisions on capital gains (Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024)

questions.q: Rule of 72 at 12%:
questions.why: By the Rule of 72, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years at 12%.

questions.q: SIP stands for:
questions.why: SIP stands for systematic investment plan, regular fixed investments, usually monthly.

questions.q: Lower-cost mutual fund plan:
questions.why: Direct plans are lower cost because they have no commission. Regular plans include distributor fees.

questions.q: Bank deposit insurance limit:
questions.why: Bank deposit insurance by DICGC covers up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.

questions.q: Equity is best for:
questions.why: Equity is best for long-term goals, because its volatility evens out over time. It is a poor home for rent, daily expenses or an emergency fund.

questions.q: ELSS lock-in:
questions.why: ELSS has a 3-year lock-in.

questions.q: ₹2 lakh at 9% doubles in about:
questions.why: At 9%, the Rule of 72 gives 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years to double.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Stopping SIPs in a market fall is wise. Reason (R): SIPs buy more units when prices are low.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: SIPs buy more units when prices are low, so a fall is a buying opportunity for long-term investors, not a reason to stop.

questions.q: LTCG ₹3,00,000 on equity in a year: tax (before cess)?
Real return if FD gives 7% and inflation is 6%:
questions.why: Real return ≈ nominal − inflation = 7% − 6% ≈ 1%.

questions.q: Case: SIP ₹4,000/month at NAV ₹40, ₹20, ₹80. Average cost per unit?
questions.why: Units bought: ₹4,000 at ₹40 is 100, at ₹20 is 200, at ₹80 is 50, so 350 units for ₹12,000. Average cost = 12,000 ÷ 350 ≈ ₹34.29.

questions.q: Case: 30-year-old, retirement goal, moderate risk. Sensible allocation?
questions.why: A 30-year-old with a long horizon and moderate risk suits roughly 60–75% equity with the rest in debt or gold, rebalanced yearly. All small-cap, all FD or one stock is too risky or too conservative.

questions.q: Case: A 'SEBI-certified' WhatsApp adviser asks for your demat OTP. Action?
questions.why: Never share your demat OTP. Refuse, verify registration with SEBI and report it, since these are scam signs.

questions.q: ₹5 lakh for 20 years: 12% vs 10.5% net. Approximate difference? (1.12²⁰≈9.65, 1.105²⁰≈7.36)
questions.why: ₹5 lakh grows to 5 × 9.65 = ₹48.25 lakh at 12% and 5 × 7.36 = ₹36.8 lakh at 10.5%. The difference is about ₹11.45 lakh, around ₹11.5 lakh.

questions.q: Why are index funds often recommended for beginners?
options: Low cost, broad diversification, no need to pick managers
questions.why: Index funds are often recommended for beginners because of low cost, broad diversification and no need to pick fund managers. They still carry market risk.

courses.title: Employee money · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: A formula and numbers sheet, a mixed calculation drill, and a full mock test across salary, benefits, tax, debt and investing.
outcomes: Learners can recall key formulas and limits
Learners can solve mixed money calculations
Learners can score 80%+ on the mock

scenes.text: Sara pins one page above her desk.
It answers 90% of her money questions.

steps.title: Salary & benefits
steps.body:
- Net = gross − (PF + PT + TDS + others)
- PF: 12% employee; employer 12% → EPS 8.33% of ≤₹15,000 (max ₹1,250) + rest to EPF
- Gratuity = 15 × last (basic+DA) × years ÷ 26; >6 months rounds up; ₹20 L limit
- PPF: 15 yrs, ₹500–₹1.5 L/yr; NPS: ≥40% annuity at 60

steps.title: Debt & investing
steps.body:
- EMI = P·r·(1+r)ⁿ ÷ [(1+r)ⁿ − 1]
- A = P(1+r)ⁿ; Rule of 72
- Emergency fund 3–6 months (6–12 if risky)
- Card utilisation < 30%; scores 300–900
- Equity LTCG 12.5% above ₹1.25 L; STCG 20%
- DICGC ₹5 lakh

quiz.why: The old-regime 80C limit is ₹1.5 lakh.
In the new regime, income between ₹12 and ₹16 lakh is taxed at 15%.
The tax-free gratuity limit is ₹20 lakh.
DICGC covers deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.

scenes.text: Five quick calculations, one coffee.
Check each with the formula sheet.

steps.title: Drill 1: PF
steps.body: Basic ₹20,000 → employee ₹2,400; employer ₹2,400 → EPS ₹1,250, EPF ₹1,150 → into EPF ₹3,550/month.

steps.title: Drill 4: Compounding
steps.body: ₹50,000 at 8% for 9 years ≈ doubles (Rule of 72) → ≈ ₹1,00,000 (exact 1.08⁹ ≈ 1.999).

activity.prompt: New regime: salary ₹14,75,000 (taxable ₹14 L). Tax including 4% cess?

quiz.why: Employee EPF is 12% of ₹20,000 = ₹2,400. The employer's 12% is also ₹2,400, of which ₹1,250 goes to EPS, leaving ₹1,150. Total into EPF = 2,400 + 1,150 = ₹3,550.

quiz.q: New regime taxable ₹16 L tax before cess:

quiz.why: At 8%, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years, so ₹50,000 becomes about ₹1,00,000.

scenes.text: Attempt the mock in 25 minutes with a calculator.
Redo any chapter where you lose two or more marks.

steps.title: Calculation habits
steps.body: Write the formula, plug numbers, compute slab by slab, add cess last, sanity-check (is tax < 30% of income?).

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Numbers here are for FY 2025-26 and current rules at writing; Budgets and the new Income-tax Act, 2025 can change them. This is general education, not financial or tax advice.

steps.title: Action plan
steps.body: This month: check payslip and PF passbook, set up a budget with automatic savings, start or review an emergency fund, compare tax regimes.

activity.prompt: My money actions this month
items: Checked my payslip and PF passbook
Set an automatic saving on salary day

quiz.why: Cess is applied after computing slab tax, as 4% of the tax, not on income.

options: It should be well below 30% of income for most
quiz.why: A sanity check is that tax should be well below 30% of income for most people, since the effective rate is lower than the top slab rate.
Tax numbers may change with budgets and new laws, so check current rules.

questions.q: CTC includes employer PF:
questions.why: CTC usually includes employer PF, so it is more than the money you receive.

questions.q: Employee PF rate:
questions.why: The employee PF rate is 12% of basic (plus DA).

questions.q: ITR usual due date (salaried):
questions.why: The usual ITR due date for salaried employees is 31 July.

questions.q: Pay full card bill:
questions.why: Paying the full card bill by the due date means no interest is charged.

questions.q: PPF max per year:
questions.why: The maximum PPF deposit is ₹1.5 lakh per year.

questions.q: New regime nil-tax taxable income (FY 2025-26):
questions.why: For FY 2025-26, the new regime gives nil tax up to ₹12 L taxable income because of the 87A rebate.

questions.q: Old regime top rate:
questions.why: The old-regime top rate is 30%, on income above ₹10 L.

questions.q: Rule of 72 at 8%:
questions.why: By the Rule of 72, money doubles in 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years at 8%.

questions.q: Gratuity: basic ₹52,000, 6 years 9 months:
questions.why: 6 years 9 months rounds up to 7 years, so gratuity = 15 × ₹52,000 × 7 ÷ 26 = ₹2,10,000.

questions.q: Assertion (A): HRA exemption reduces tax in the new regime. Reason (R): The new regime disallows most exemptions.
questions.why: The assertion is false because HRA exemption isn't available in the new regime; the reason is true, since the new regime disallows most exemptions.

questions.q: Basic ₹35,000 → employer EPF share (after EPS):
questions.why: Employer's 12% of ₹35,000 is ₹4,200. After the EPS share of ₹1,250 (8.33% of ₹15,000), the EPF share is ₹2,950.

questions.q: Equity LTCG ₹1,75,000 in a year → tax before cess:
Case: Old regime taxable ₹7,00,000. Tax incl. cess?
Case: Salary ₹13 L in new regime (taxable ₹12.25 L). Which is right?
options: Tax applies above ₹12 L with marginal relief limiting tax to the excess over ₹12 L
questions.why: Taxable ₹12.25 L is just above ₹12 L, so the rebate no longer applies in full. Marginal relief limits the tax to the excess over ₹12 L, which is ₹25,000.

questions.q: Case: ₹8 lakh loan, 10% p.a., 3 years — which is TRUE?
options: Total interest is more than zero and falls if you prepay early
questions.why: A ₹8 lakh loan at 10% over 3 years has positive total interest, which falls if you prepay early. EMI is not just ₹8 lakh ÷ 36, and longer tenure raises total interest.

questions.q: Case: You have ₹60,000 card debt at 3.5%/month and ₹60,000 in an FD at 7% p.a. (not emergency money). Best?
questions.why: Break the FD and clear the card, since the card costs about 42% a year (3.5% a month) while the FD earns 7%.

questions.q: New regime, salary ₹22,75,000 (taxable ₹22 L). Tax incl. cess?
Which statement about EPS is correct?
options: Employer's 8.33% is on wages capped at ₹15,000; pension needs 10 years' service
questions.why: The employer's 8.33% goes to EPS on wages capped at ₹15,000, and a pension needs 10 years' service. The employee's 12% goes to EPF, not EPS.

questions.q: SIP ₹3,000 at NAVs ₹30, ₹15, ₹60. Units bought?
questions.why: Units: ₹3,000 at ₹30 is 100, at ₹15 is 200, and at ₹60 is 50. The total is 350 units.

questions.q: Best overall order of money priorities for a new employee?
options: Budget & emergency fund → insurance → clear costly debt → invest for goals
questions.why: The sensible order is budget and emergency fund, then insurance, then clearing costly debt, then investing for goals. Building the foundation first protects you.

corp-management.title: Management, leadership and workplace communication
corp-management.description: Chapter-by-chapter people leadership: becoming a manager, 1:1s, feedback and coaching, goals and performance, motivating and leading teams, workplace communication, and decisions and leadership styles.

courses.title: Ch 1 · From individual contributor to manager
courses.summary: What managers actually do, how to delegate well, how to manage your time and priorities, and a plan for your first 90 days leading a team.
outcomes: Learners can describe the shift from doing to enabling
Learners can choose what and how to delegate
Learners can prioritise with the Eisenhower matrix
Learners can write a 30-60-90 day plan as a new manager

scenes.text: Priya, the team's best engineer, is promoted to manager. She keeps taking the hardest tickets herself.
Six weeks later her team is blocked, waiting for her reviews, and she's working till midnight.
Her mentor says: 'Your output is now your team's output.'

steps.title: The big shift
steps.body: As an individual contributor (IC), success = **your** work. As a manager, success = **your team's results and growth**. Your main tools become: setting direction, hiring and developing people, removing blockers, making decisions, and communicating up, down and across.

steps.title: Core responsibilities
steps.body:
- **Clarity:** goals, priorities, roles
- **People:** hiring, 1:1s, feedback, coaching, growth, recognition
- **Execution:** plans, risks, removing blockers, quality
- **Communication:** updates to stakeholders, context to the team
- **Culture:** safety, fairness, standards

steps.title: Solved example: Priya's reset
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Stop owning critical-path tickets; pair on hard problems instead.
**Step 2:** Weekly 1:1s with each person.
**Step 3:** Review rota so reviews aren't all on her.
**Step 4:** Block 'maker time' for strategy and stakeholder work.
**Result:** team throughput rises; she works normal hours.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Being the 'super-IC' bottleneck.
- Avoiding hard conversations to stay liked.
- Managing everyone the same way regardless of experience.

activity.prompt: IC habit or manager habit?

items.text: Taking the hardest task yourself every time
Rewriting team members' work at night
Measuring your day by your own commits

quiz.why: A manager's output is mainly the team's results and growth. Meetings and personal tasks are only means.
Super-IC managers, who keep doing the work themselves, often become bottlenecks because everything waits for them.

quiz.q: Which is a core manager responsibility?
quiz.why: Giving feedback and coaching is a core manager responsibility, as it develops people. Hiding problems or avoiding decisions is not.
Managing everyone identically ignores their different skill and experience levels. Good managers adapt to the person.

quiz.q: Blocking 'maker time' as a manager helps with:
quiz.why: Blocking 'maker time' gives managers uninterrupted time for strategy and planning work.

story.title: I'll just do it, it's faster

scenes.text: Arun says delegating takes longer than doing it himself.
By the third time, his team member does it faster than him — and Arun has time for planning.

steps.title: What to delegate
steps.body: Delegate: recurring tasks, tasks that grow someone's skills, work others can do 80% as well. Keep: confidential people issues, final accountability, tasks only you are authorised to do.

steps.title: Levels of delegation
steps.body:
1) **Do as I say** (follow instructions)
2) **Research and report** options
3) **Recommend** — I decide
4) **Decide and tell me**
5) **Decide; no need to tell me**
Match the level to the person's skill and the task's risk; increase over time.

steps.title: Solved example: a clear hand-off
steps.body: Arun to Meena: 'Please own the weekly client report from next week (**what**). It helps the client track SLAs (**why**). Draft it by Thursday 4 pm (**when**); use last month's template (**how/resources**). You decide the format; send me the draft the first two weeks, then just send it (**level 3 → 4**). Ask me anytime.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Dumping' tasks without context or authority.
- Taking work back at the first mistake.
- Delegating only boring work, never growth opportunities.
- Delegating responsibility but not accountability — you still own the outcome.

activity.prompt: Order the delegation levels from least to most autonomy.

options: What, why, when, resources and authority level
quiz.why: A good hand-off covers what, why, when, the resources and the level of authority. A deadline alone leaves too much unclear.
When delegating, accountability stays with the manager, because you still own the outcome. Only the task is handed over.
Delegating only boring tasks misses growth opportunities. People develop by taking on meaningful work.

quiz.q: Taking work back after the first mistake:
quiz.why: Taking work back after the first mistake undermines learning and trust. Coach instead.

options: Brand-new hire on a high-risk task
quiz.why: 'Decide and tell me' suits an experienced person on a moderate-risk task. A new hire on a high-risk task needs more direction.

scenes.text: Rakesh spends his day on urgent emails and pings; the hiring plan due next week isn't started.
He draws four boxes and sorts his work.

steps.title: Eisenhower matrix
steps.body:
- **Urgent + important:** do now (production incident, deadline today).
- **Important, not urgent:** **schedule** — planning, hiring, coaching, learning (where managers create most value).
- **Urgent, not important:** delegate or batch (many pings, some requests).
- **Neither:** drop.

steps.title: Practical habits
steps.body:
- Weekly planning: top 3 outcomes.
- Calendar blocks for important-not-urgent work.
- Batch email/chat at set times.
- Say 'not now' with a date: 'I can look at this Thursday.'

steps.title: Solved example: sort Rakesh's list
steps.body: Incident at a key client → **Do**. Hiring plan due next week → **Schedule** (2 h tomorrow). Request to forward a deck → **Delegate**. Reading every all-company thread → **Drop/skim**. Coaching a struggling report → **Schedule** this week.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Living in the urgent box.
- Never protecting time for 1:1s and planning.

activity.prompt: Place each task in the Eisenhower matrix.

quiz.q: Important but not urgent work should be:
quiz.why: Important but not urgent work should be scheduled, so it gets protected time before it becomes urgent.

quiz.q: Most managerial value usually sits in:
quiz.why: Most managerial value sits in the important, not urgent quadrant, such as planning and people development.
Urgent but not important tasks should be delegated or batched, which reduces interruptions.
Saying 'not now' well includes a concrete alternative time, which keeps a respectful boundary.
Plan your week around your top 3 outcomes, to keep focus.

lessons.title: Your first 90 days as a manager

scenes.text: Kiran is promoted to lead the team she was part of — including her close friend.
She writes a 30-60-90 plan to start well.

steps.title: 30-60-90 plan
steps.body:
- **Days 1–30: Listen and learn.** 1:1 with each person (goals, frustrations, ideas), meet stakeholders, understand metrics and processes.
- **Days 31–60: Small wins and clarity.** Share what you heard, agree team priorities and working norms, fix 1–2 quick pain points.
- **Days 61–90: Direction.** Set goals/OKRs, development plans, rhythms (1:1s, reviews), and a roadmap.

steps.title: Managing former peers and friends
steps.body: Acknowledge the change openly: 'Our relationship changes a bit — I'll be fair to everyone, and I'll still value your honesty.' Avoid favouritism (and its appearance) in assignments, ratings and information.

steps.title: Solved example: first 1:1 questions
steps.body:
- What's going well, and what's frustrating?
- What should I keep, stop, start?
- How do you like to receive feedback?
- What are your career goals for the next 1–2 years?
- What do you need from me?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing everything in week one.
- Gossiping with old friends about team members.
- Not asking your own manager what success looks like.

activity.prompt: New manager's first 30 days
items: Met my manager to agree success criteria
Read team metrics and recent incidents

quiz.why: In days 1–30, listen and learn so you understand the team before making changes. Reorganising or firing early is premature.

options: Acknowledge the change and be visibly fair
quiz.why: With former peers, acknowledge the change and be visibly fair. Pretending nothing changed or favouring friends damages trust.

options: What do you need from me?
quiz.why: 'What do you need from me?' opens dialogue in a first 1:1. Questions about complaints or salary don't.
Ask your own manager what success looks like, so you are aligned on expectations.
Quick wins in days 31–60 build credibility and momentum.

questions.q: A manager's success is measured mostly by:
questions.why: A manager's success is measured mostly by team outcomes, not emails or personal tasks.

questions.q: Eisenhower 'neither urgent nor important':
questions.why: In the Eisenhower matrix, tasks that are neither urgent nor important should be dropped.

questions.q: First 30 days as a new manager:
questions.why: In the first 30 days as a new manager, listen and learn before changing things.

questions.q: Which should usually NOT be delegated?
questions.why: Confidential people decisions are part of the manager's role and shouldn't be delegated. Data collation, reports and meeting notes can be.

questions.q: 'Recommend; I decide' is delegation level:
questions.why: 'Recommend; I decide' is the middle delegation level, level 3, where the report proposes and the manager decides.

questions.q: Planning and coaching are typically:
questions.why: Planning and coaching are important but not urgent, so you schedule them.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Delegation moves accountability to the team member. Reason (R): Managers remain responsible for outcomes.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: managers remain responsible for outcomes, so delegation doesn't move accountability to the team member.

questions.q: A good hand-off includes all EXCEPT:
questions.why: A good hand-off shares the purpose, the what, when and authority level. Hiding the purpose is what it should not do.

questions.q: Super-IC behaviour causes:
questions.why: Super-IC behaviour causes bottlenecks and burnout, since the manager becomes a single point everything depends on.

questions.q: Case: New manager's friend expects the best projects. Best response?
options: Explain assignments are based on fit and fairness; offer growth openly
questions.why: Explain that assignments are based on fit and fairness, and offer growth openly. Giving a friend everything or avoiding them is unfair.

questions.q: Case: You spend 80% of time in urgent pings. Best change?
options: Batch messages, delegate, block time for important work
questions.why: With 80% of time in urgent pings, batch messages, delegate and block time for important work. Working weekends or answering faster doesn't fix it.

questions.q: Case: A junior made an error on a delegated report. Best response?
options: Review together, explain, keep the task with closer check-ins
questions.why: Review the error together, explain, and keep the task with closer check-ins. Taking it back forever or criticising publicly harms learning.

questions.q: Case: Day 10 as manager — you want to change the team's process. Best?
options: Listen first; propose changes after understanding why it exists
questions.why: On day 10, listen first and propose changes after understanding why the process exists. Changing it today may remove something that serves a purpose.

questions.q: Which BEST shows you've moved from IC to manager mindset?
options: Measuring your week by team blockers removed and people grown
questions.why: Measuring your week by team blockers removed and people grown shows a manager mindset focused on leverage. Hours, tickets or code lines are IC measures.

questions.q: Which delegation level for an experienced engineer on a low-risk, recurring task?
questions.why: For an experienced engineer on a low-risk, recurring task, 'decide; no need to report' fits, since it gives maximum autonomy.

courses.title: Ch 2 · 1:1s, feedback and coaching
courses.summary: Running useful one-on-ones, giving feedback with the SBI model, coaching with GROW, and receiving feedback and recognising people well.
outcomes: Learners can run a 1:1 that the team member owns
Learners can give specific, behaviour-based feedback with SBI
Learners can coach using GROW questions
Learners can receive feedback without defensiveness and give meaningful recognition

scenes.text: Deepak's 1:1s are just task status. His best engineer resigns, saying she 'never felt heard'.
He redesigns his 1:1s around the person, not the tasks.

steps.title: Purpose
steps.body: A 1:1 is **the team member's meeting**: their priorities, blockers, growth, wellbeing and feedback both ways. Status belongs in standups or dashboards.

steps.title: A simple structure (30 min, weekly or fortnightly)
steps.body:
1) Their topics first (shared running doc)
2) Blockers and support needed
3) Feedback both ways
4) Growth/career (at least monthly)
5) Actions and owners

steps.title: Solved example: good questions
steps.body:
- 'What's on your mind this week?'
- 'What's slowing you down that I can remove?'
- 'What's one thing I could do better as your manager?'
- 'Which work energised you recently?'
- 'How are you, really — workload okay?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cancelling 1:1s whenever busy — signals people aren't a priority.
- Talking 80% of the time.
- No notes or follow-up on promised actions.

activity.prompt: 1:1 health check
items: Recurring 1:1 on the calendar with each report
Shared agenda document they can add to
They speak more than I do
I ask for feedback on myself
Actions are written and followed up

options: The team member's priorities, growth and blockers
quiz.why: A 1:1 is mainly for the team member's priorities, growth and blockers. It is their meeting, not a status report.
Frequent cancellations signal that people aren't a priority, even if you meant no harm.

quiz.q: Who should talk more in a 1:1?
quiz.why: The team member should talk more in a 1:1, while the manager listens.
Career topics should come up regularly, for example monthly, not only at appraisal or exit.
Status updates belong in standups or dashboards, which frees 1:1 time for people topics.

scenes.text: Rina's manager tells her, 'You're not a team player.' She has no idea what to change.
A different manager uses SBI — and Rina knows exactly what to do.

steps.title: SBI model
steps.body:
The **Situation–Behaviour–Impact** model (popularised by the Center for Creative Leadership):
- **Situation:** when and where
- **Behaviour:** what the person did or said (observable, not labels)
- **Impact:** the effect on you, the team, the customer
Then invite their view and agree a next step.

steps.title: Solved example: corrective feedback
steps.body:
**Label (unhelpful):** 'You're not a team player.'
**SBI:** 'In Tuesday's sprint review (S), you interrupted Aman three times while he presented (B). He stopped sharing his ideas and we lost his input on the design (I). What was going on for you? Next time, could you note questions and ask at the end?'

steps.title: Solved example: positive feedback
steps.body: 'In yesterday's client call (S), you summarised the three open risks and owners in two minutes (B). The client said it was the clearest update they'd had, and we got sign-off a week early (I). Please keep doing that in every call.'

steps.title: Timing and ratio
steps.body: Give feedback **soon**, **privately** for corrective feedback, and much more often for things done well. Make it about behaviour, never personality.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The 'feedback sandwich' that hides the message.
- Saving feedback for the annual review.
- Using 'always/never'.

activity.prompt: Label each part of the SBI statement.
pairs: '…you presented the budget without the cost breakdown…'
'…so the CFO couldn't approve it and we lost a week.'
'Let's add a breakdown slide by Thursday.'

quiz.why: SBI stands for Situation, Behaviour, Impact, a feedback model.

quiz.q: Which is a behaviour (not a label)?
options: 'You arrived 20 minutes late to the client call'
quiz.why: 'You arrived 20 minutes late to the client call' is an observable behaviour. 'Lazy', 'unprofessional' and 'bad attitude' are labels.
Corrective feedback works best soon after the event and in private. Public or late feedback is less relevant and less respectful.
After SBI, invite their perspective, to make it a dialogue rather than a verdict.
Positive feedback should be specific and frequent, so it reinforces the behaviour you want.

story.title: Just tell me what to do

scenes.text: Sahil keeps bringing problems to his manager expecting answers.
His manager starts asking questions instead — and Sahil starts solving problems himself.

steps.title: The GROW model
steps.body:
Developed by Sir John Whitmore and colleagues:
- **Goal:** What do you want to achieve?
- **Reality:** What's happening now? What have you tried?
- **Options:** What could you do? What else?
- **Will (way forward):** What will you do, by when? How committed are you (1–10)?

steps.title: Solved example: a coaching conversation
steps.body:
**G:** 'What would a good outcome be for the vendor delay?' → 'Delivery by the 20th.'
**R:** 'Where are things now?' → 'They're short of testers.'
**O:** 'What options do you see?' → 'Lend our tester; cut scope; escalate.'
**W:** 'Which will you do and when?' → 'Offer our tester for 3 days and agree scope by Friday.'

steps.title: Coach vs tell
steps.body: **Tell** when there's a crisis, a safety issue, or the person is new and lacks basic knowledge. **Coach** when the person has some capability and the goal is growth and ownership.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leading questions that are disguised instructions.
- Skipping 'Will' — no commitment, no action.
- Coaching during an emergency.

activity.prompt: Match the question to the GROW stage.
pairs: 'What do you want to achieve by month-end?'
'What will you do first, and by when?'
'On a scale of 1–10, how committed are you?'

quiz.why: GROW was developed by Sir John Whitmore and colleagues.
In GROW, R stands for Reality, asking about the current situation.

options: The person has capability and growth is the goal
quiz.why: Coach rather than tell when the person has capability and growth is the goal. Use telling for day one, safety issues or emergencies.
Skipping the 'Will' stage leaves no commitment to act, so nothing may change.
Good coaching questions are open-ended, which prompts exploration. Yes/no, leading or accusatory questions don't.

scenes.text: Neha's team survey says she 'doesn't recognise effort'. Her first reaction is to explain why they're wrong.
Instead she thanks them, asks for examples and changes one habit.

steps.title: Receiving feedback
steps.body: 1) **Listen** fully. 2) **Thank** the person — it took courage. 3) **Clarify** with examples. 4) **Reflect** before responding. 5) **Act** and tell them what you changed. You don't have to agree with everything, but you do have to consider it.

steps.title: Recognition that lands
steps.body: Specific (what and why it mattered), timely, sincere, and fair across the team. Some people like public praise; others prefer private notes — ask. Recognise effort and learning, not just big wins.

steps.title: Solved example: specific recognition
steps.body:
Generic: 'Great job, team!'
Specific: 'Farhan, staying calm during last night's outage and writing clear updates every 30 minutes kept the client informed and avoided an escalation. Thank you.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Defensiveness: 'Yes, but…'.
- Recognising only the loudest people.
- Asking for feedback and never acting on it.

a.text: A team member says, 'In meetings, you often cut people off.' Your response?

choices.label: 'That's not true, I just keep meetings efficient.'
'Thank you for telling me. Can you give me an example?'

b.text: They go quiet. Months later you learn others felt the same. Try again?

choices.label: Go back, apologise, and ask for examples

c.text: They share two examples. What next?

choices.label: Commit to a change and ask them to flag it if it happens again
Say thanks and change nothing

d.text: A month later the team says meetings feel more open. You thank them for the feedback publicly.

e.text: People stop giving you feedback. Lesson: act on what you hear.

quiz.why: When receiving feedback, first listen fully to understand it. Defending or countering shuts the conversation down.
Effective recognition is specific and timely, so the person knows what was valued.

options: Act and tell them what changed
quiz.why: After feedback, act on it and tell them what changed. This closes the loop.
'Yes, but…' signals defensiveness, since it dismisses what came before the 'but'.
People differ, so ask the person's preference about public or private praise.

questions.q: SBI 'I' stands for:
questions.why: In SBI, I stands for Impact, the effect of the behaviour.

questions.q: GROW 'O' stands for:
questions.why: In GROW, O stands for Options. The stages are Goal, Reality, Options and Will.

questions.q: Whose meeting is a 1:1?
questions.why: A 1:1 is the team member's meeting, so they own the agenda.

questions.q: Which is behaviour-based feedback?
options: 'You missed the 5 pm deadline twice this week'
questions.why: 'You missed the 5 pm deadline twice this week' is specific, observable behaviour. 'Careless' or 'don't care' are labels.

questions.q: Coaching suits:
questions.why: Coaching suits building ownership in capable people. Day-one hires, emergencies and safety issues need direction.

questions.q: Recognition should be:
questions.why: Recognition should be specific, because it shows what was valued and lands better.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The feedback sandwich always works best. Reason (R): Hiding the main point between praise can blur the message.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: the feedback sandwich can hide the main point between praise and blur the message.

questions.q: 'What have you tried so far?' is GROW stage:
questions.why: 'What have you tried so far?' explores the current situation, so it is the Reality stage of GROW.

questions.q: A 1:1 dominated by task status:
questions.why: A 1:1 dominated by task status misses growth and wellbeing topics. Status can be shared elsewhere.

questions.q: Case: Team member's code reviews are harsh and others avoid asking him. Best SBI?
options: 'In last week's reviews (S), comments like "this is junk" (B) made two juniors stop asking you (I). What's your view?'
questions.why: The SBI statement names the situation, the behaviour (the specific comment) and its impact, then invites his view. 'You're toxic' is a label, and ignoring it lets it continue.

questions.q: Case: During a production outage, a junior asks what to do. Best approach?
options: Tell clearly now; coach in the retro later
questions.why: In a production outage, tell clearly now and coach in the retro later. Crisis calls for direction, not 20 minutes of questions.

questions.q: Case: You receive feedback you disagree with. Best?
options: Thank, ask for examples, reflect, then respond thoughtfully
questions.why: Thank them, ask for examples, reflect, then respond thoughtfully. Arguing or retaliating wastes useful information.

questions.q: Which combination best improves 1:1s?
options: Shared agenda, their topics first, regular growth talk, written actions
questions.why: Good 1:1s have a shared agenda, put their topics first, discuss growth regularly and record actions. Manager monologues, status-only or cancelled meetings don't.

questions.q: Why is specific recognition more motivating than generic praise?
options: It shows you noticed what mattered and reinforces that exact behaviour
questions.why: Specific recognition shows you noticed what mattered and reinforces that exact behaviour. Generic praise doesn't tell people what to repeat.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Goals, OKRs and performance
courses.summary: Writing SMART goals, setting OKRs, handling performance conversations and underperformance fairly, and reducing bias in reviews and calibration.
outcomes: Learners can rewrite vague goals as SMART goals
Learners can write objectives with measurable key results
Learners can run a fair underperformance process
Learners can spot and reduce common rating biases

scenes.text: A support team's goal is 'improve customer satisfaction'. At year end, nobody knows if they did.
Next year they write it SMART.

steps.title: SMART
steps.body:
- **Specific:** what exactly
- **Measurable:** how you'll know
- **Achievable:** stretching but realistic
- **Relevant:** linked to team/company priorities
- **Time-bound:** by when

steps.title: Solved example: rewrite
steps.body:
Vague: 'Improve customer satisfaction.'
SMART: 'Raise CSAT for chat support from 78% to 85% by 31 March by cutting first-response time from 6 to 2 minutes and publishing 20 new help articles.'

steps.title: Solved example: a personal growth goal
steps.body:
Vague: 'Get better at presenting.'
SMART: 'Present the team's monthly update to leadership in 3 of the next 4 months, with feedback scores of 4/5 or higher, after completing the internal presentation workshop by 15 May.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Activities instead of outcomes ('hold 10 meetings').
- Too many goals — aim for 3–5.
- Goals no one revisits until appraisal.

activity.prompt: SMART or not?

items.text: Reduce invoice errors from 4% to 1% by Q3
Launch the Hindi app version to 100% of users by 30 June
Close 12 enterprise deals worth ₹6 crore this financial year

quiz.why: In SMART, M stands for Measurable.
'Be more proactive' is vague, so it fails mainly on being specific and measurable.
A good number of goals is 3 to 5, which keeps focus.
Goals should focus on outcomes, the results achieved, not just hours, meetings or activity.
In SMART, T stands for Time-bound, meaning there is a deadline.

scenes.text: A product team ships 40 features in a quarter but user retention doesn't change.
They switch to OKRs focused on outcomes.

steps.title: Objectives and Key Results
steps.body:
- **Objective:** qualitative, inspiring direction ('Make onboarding effortless for new users').
- **Key Results (2–5):** measurable outcomes that prove progress ('Day-7 retention from 32% to 40%', 'Time to first value under 5 minutes', 'Onboarding support tickets down 30%').
- **Initiatives:** the projects you'll do to move the KRs (not KRs themselves).

steps.title: Committed vs aspirational
steps.body: **Committed** OKRs are expected to be fully met. **Aspirational** (stretch) OKRs aim high; achieving ~70% can be a good result. Be clear which is which, and don't tie stretch OKRs directly to individual ratings, or people will sandbag.

steps.title: Solved example: fix a bad KR
steps.body:
Bad KR: 'Launch new onboarding flow' (that's an initiative/output).
Better KR: 'Increase onboarding completion from 55% to 75%.'
Scoring: completion reaches 70% → (70−55)/(75−55) = **0.75**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing tasks as KRs.
- Too many OKRs.
- Setting and forgetting — review weekly or fortnightly.

activity.prompt: KR: increase NPS from 30 to 50. You reach 44. Score (0–1, two decimals)?

quiz.why: A Key Result must be measurable, so progress can be proved. A task or vague aim isn't a KR.
'Launch feature X' is an output, usually an initiative rather than a Key Result. A KR measures the outcome it should achieve.
Typically 2 to 5 key results per objective keeps it focused.
Aspirational OKRs scored around 70% can be a good result, since stretch goals aren't expected to be fully met.
OKRs should be reviewed regularly, weekly or fortnightly, so you can steer. Annual-only review is too late.

scenes.text: Vivek receives a low rating at year-end — the first he's heard of any problem.
His new manager commits: 'No surprises, ever.'

steps.title: No surprises
steps.body: If someone is shocked by their review, the manager failed earlier. Give feedback continuously; reviews should summarise conversations already held.

steps.title: Fair underperformance process
steps.body:
1) **Diagnose:** skill, will, clarity, or circumstances (health, family, workload)?
2) **Clarify expectations** in writing with examples.
3) **Support:** training, pairing, resources, check-ins.
4) **Agree a time-bound plan** with measurable goals (a performance improvement plan, if used, must be genuine — a path to success, not a paper trail to exit).
5) **Review** regularly and document.
