scenes.text: In an informal team WhatsApp group, someone jokes about the manager's 'stupid decisions'. Vikas adds a laughing emoji.
A week later, a screenshot reaches the manager.

steps.title: Assume everything is public
steps.body: Anything typed in a group can be screenshotted and forwarded. Informal groups with colleagues are still **work relationships**.

steps.title: Handling gossip
steps.body:
- Don't add to it — silence or a neutral reply.
- Redirect: 'Not sure, better to ask them directly.'
- Don't forward unverified news (reorg rumours, layoff lists).
- Leave groups that become toxic, politely ('Muting work groups after hours').

steps.title: Solved example: a rumour arrives
steps.body:
Message: 'Heard 20% layoffs next week, list attached!'
**Step 1:** Don't forward.
**Step 2:** Don't speculate.
**Step 3:** If worried, ask your manager or HR for clarity privately.
**Step 4:** If the 'list' contains personal data, it may be a confidentiality breach — report it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Emoji reactions count as participation.
- Sharing someone's personal life or health news.
- Venting about clients in groups that include vendors.

a.text: In the team WhatsApp group, a colleague mocks a new joiner's accent. Others laugh. What do you do?

choices.label: Add a laughing emoji to fit in
Post a neutral redirect, then check on the new joiner privately

b.text: The new joiner sees it and complains to HR with screenshots, including your emoji. What now?

choices.label: Apologise sincerely to the new joiner and don't repeat it

c.text: The new joiner thanks you. Later the same colleague tries to start more gossip. What do you do?

choices.label: Mute the group after hours and avoid gossip threads
Gossip about the colleague in another group

d.text: You're seen as trustworthy — the person people come to, not the one people fear in screenshots.

e.text: The cycle continues and eventually reaches you. Lesson: step out of gossip entirely.

quiz.why: Messages in informal work groups can be screenshotted and forwarded, so assume they are public.

quiz.q: An emoji reaction to mockery is:
quiz.why: An emoji reaction to mockery counts as participation, signalling approval.
Unverified layoff rumours should not be forwarded, because they can harm people.
A neutral redirect like 'Better to ask them directly' defuses gossip without joining it.

quiz.q: A layoff 'list' with names may be:
quiz.why: A layoff 'list' with names may be a confidentiality breach that should be reported.

scenes.text: Rahul and Divya build a dashboard together. In the review, Rahul says, 'I built this dashboard.'
Divya fumes. She wants to handle it without a war.

steps.title: Prevent it
steps.body:
- Agree roles upfront: 'You do data, I do UI; we present together.'
- Keep a visible trail: tickets, commits, docs with names.
- Share progress in team channels.

steps.title: In the moment
steps.body: Add naturally and calmly: 'Yes — Rahul did the data pipeline, and I built the visualisations. Happy to walk through the filters.' This corrects without attacking.

steps.title: Solved example: the private talk
steps.body: 'Rahul, in the review it sounded like you built the whole dashboard. I did the UI and filters. Next time, can we present our parts together?' — If it continues, mention the facts to your manager with evidence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Public accusations.
- Refusing to collaborate ever again — collaboration is still valuable; set clearer terms.
- Over-documenting to the point of paranoia.

a.text: In a demo, your peer says 'I built this', though you built half. What do you say?

choices.label: 'That's not true! I did most of it.'
'Yes, and I built the filters and charts — let me show those.'

b.text: Leaders look uncomfortable. Your peer looks hurt. What now?

choices.label: Apologise for the tone and talk privately later

c.text: After the demo, what's next?

choices.label: Privately agree to present together next time; keep tickets updated with names
Complain to the whole team

d.text: Next demo, you present together. Your manager notices both contributions.

e.text: The team takes sides; your manager sees conflict, not your work. Lesson: correct calmly, then fix the process.

options: Agree roles and keep a visible trail
quiz.why: Credit theft is best prevented by agreeing roles and keeping a visible trail.
A calm correction like 'Yes, and I built the charts…' adds to the credit without attacking.

quiz.q: If it continues after a private talk:
quiz.why: If it continues after a private talk, share facts with your manager.
Visible trails include tickets, commits and docs, which serve as evidence.
Refusing all future collaboration hurts you too. Set terms instead.

scenes.text: Whenever Meera presents, a peer adds, 'Just to be safe, let's double-check her numbers.'
It sounds helpful — but it's every time, and only with her.

steps.title: Spot the pattern
steps.body: Undermining often looks small: doubting your work publicly, leaving you off emails, 'forgetting' to pass information, taking over your meetings, backhanded compliments. One incident may be innocent; a **pattern** isn't.

steps.title: Respond with evidence and calm
steps.body: 1) Note dates and examples. 2) Make your work solid and transparent (share sources). 3) Address it privately with facts: 'In the last three reviews you suggested re-checking my numbers. Is there something specific you've seen?' 4) If it continues, discuss with your manager using examples.

steps.title: Solved example: pre-empt
steps.body: Meera starts each presentation: 'Numbers are from the finance dashboard as of Monday, reconciled with Ops.' The 'double-check' comments stop having an effect.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reacting emotionally in public.
- Assuming malice from one incident.
- Not keeping notes — patterns are hard to prove from memory.

a.text: For the third time, a peer suggests in a meeting that your numbers 'need checking'. What do you do?

choices.label: Snap: 'Why do you always doubt me?'
Calmly state your sources, then talk privately later

b.text: Others see you as defensive. What now?

choices.label: Regain composure; prepare sources next time and talk privately

c.text: In private, the peer says, 'I just want accuracy.' What do you say?

choices.label: 'Me too. If you spot an issue, please tell me before the meeting so I can fix it.'
'You're jealous.'

d.text: The public comments stop. If they hadn't, you had notes to share with your manager.

e.text: The conflict escalates and your manager sees two people fighting. Lesson: stay factual.

quiz.why: Undermining is best judged by a pattern over time, not one incident or rumour.
In public, respond first with calm facts and sources, which keeps composure.
Keeping notes helps you show patterns to your manager.
A constructive norm is 'Flag issues before the meeting', which supports collaboration.
Calling someone jealous is personal and escalates conflict.

questions.q: Informal WhatsApp groups with colleagues are:
questions.why: Informal WhatsApp groups with colleagues are still work relationships, so assume they are public.

questions.q: Credit theft is best prevented by:
questions.why: Credit theft is best prevented by clear roles and visible trails.

questions.q: Discussing work in a language some can't follow:
questions.why: Discussing work in a language some can't follow excludes them.

questions.q: Neutral reply to gossip:
questions.why: 'Better to ask them directly' is a neutral reply to gossip that defuses it.

questions.q: Undermining is identified by:
questions.why: Undermining is identified by a pattern, not a single comment or instinct.

questions.q: Forwarding unverified layoff lists:
options: Harms people and may breach confidentiality
questions.why: Forwarding unverified layoff lists harms people and may breach confidentiality.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Public accusations are the best way to reclaim credit. Reason (R): Calm, additive corrections protect your reputation.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: calm, additive corrections protect your reputation better than public accusations.

questions.q: If you're in the majority language group:
options: Switch to a common language when others join
questions.why: If you are in the majority language group, switch to a common language when others join.

questions.q: Pre-empting doubts about your numbers:
questions.why: Stating sources upfront pre-empts doubts about your numbers and builds credibility.

questions.q: Case: A colleague mocks a new joiner in the group chat. Best action?
options: Neutral redirect + check on the new joiner
questions.why: Use a neutral redirect and check on the new joiner. Laughing, forwarding or ignoring it all let the mockery stand.

questions.q: Case: Your peer keeps leaving you off key emails. First step?
options: Note examples, then ask privately to be included
questions.why: Note examples, then ask privately to be included. Retaliating or accusing publicly escalates.

questions.q: Case: After a private talk, the peer still claims sole credit in demos. Next?
options: Discuss with your manager using tickets/commits as evidence
questions.why: After a private talk fails, discuss with your manager using tickets and commits as evidence. Sabotage or social media harms you.

questions.q: Case: You feel excluded by a regional group at lunch. Best long-term move?
options: Build one-to-one connections and join cross-team activities
questions.why: Build one-to-one connections and join cross-team activities to bridge the group. Eating alone or forming a rival group deepens the divide.

questions.q: Why is stepping out of gossip a political advantage?
options: People trust you with information and you avoid screenshot risk
questions.why: Stepping out of gossip is an advantage because people trust you with information and you avoid screenshot risk.

questions.q: Which response balances assertiveness and relationships when a peer takes credit?
options: 'Yes, and I built the charts — happy to show them,' then a private agreement on joint presenting
questions.why: 'Yes, and I built the charts — happy to show them,' followed by a private agreement on joint presenting is assertive and constructive. Anger or silence isn't.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Appraisals, bell curves and promotions
courses.summary: How normalisation and bell curves work, writing a strong self-appraisal, building a promotion case, and responding to an unfair rating or a low hike.
outcomes: Learners can explain forced distribution and calibration
Learners can write an evidence-based self-appraisal
Learners can build a promotion case with a sponsor
Learners can respond to an unfair rating professionally

lessons.title: Bell curves and normalisation

scenes.text: Neeraj's manager says, 'You did well, but I could only give one top rating and the curve forced the rest.'
Neeraj wants to understand how the system really works.

steps.title: Forced distribution
steps.body: Many Indian companies use **normalisation** or a **bell curve**: a fixed share of top, middle and low ratings per group (e.g. 10–20% top, 60–70% middle, 10–20% low). Managers then **calibrate** — discuss and compare people across teams to fit the distribution. Some companies have moved away from strict curves; check your company's process.

steps.title: What this means for you
steps.body: Ratings are **relative** within a pool. Your manager has to **argue** for you in calibration — so give them **evidence**. Visibility with other managers in the room matters too.

steps.title: Solved example: how many top ratings?
steps.body: Pool of 25 people, 20% top-rating limit → **5** top ratings. If 8 people performed strongly, calibration decides who gets the 5 — usually those with the clearest impact and evidence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming 'I worked hard' = top rating.
- Only showing your work in the last month before appraisal.
- Not knowing your company's rating criteria.

a.text: It's two months before appraisals. What do you do?

choices.label: Work harder quietly and hope it's noticed
choices.feedback: Your manager needs evidence to argue for you.

choices.label: Ask your manager what evidence would support a strong rating and share an impact summary

b.text: In calibration, your manager can't recall specifics, and others' managers have data. You get a middle rating. What now?

choices.label: Start a monthly impact log and share it regularly

c.text: You share a one-page impact summary with metrics. Your manager asks if other leaders know your work. What do you do?

choices.label: Offer to present your project in a cross-team review

d.text: In calibration, other managers recognise your work. Your manager secures a top rating for you.

quiz.q: In a forced distribution, ratings are:
quiz.why: In a forced distribution, ratings are relative within a pool, as on a curve.
Calibration is managers comparing and aligning ratings across teams.

quiz.q: Pool of 30, 10% top limit → top ratings:
quiz.why: A 10% top limit on a pool of 30 gives 0.10 × 30 = 3 top ratings.
Your manager needs evidence of your impact, to advocate for you.

quiz.q: Visibility with other managers matters because:
quiz.why: Visibility with other managers matters because they are in the calibration room.

sources: Performance management practice in Indian companies

scenes.text: Shruti's self-appraisal says: 'Worked on many tasks and supported the team.'
Her mentor helps her rewrite it with impact and numbers.

steps.title: STAR + numbers
steps.body: For each major achievement: **Situation/Task** (context), **Action** (what *you* did), **Result** (measurable impact). Link to goals/OKRs and company values.

steps.title: Solved example: rewrite
steps.body:
Weak: 'Worked on the payment module.'
Strong: 'Payment failures were 4.2% (S). I redesigned retry logic and added monitoring alerts (A). Failures dropped to 1.1%, saving ≈₹18 lakh/month in lost orders (R). Goal: reliability OKR — exceeded.'

steps.title: Other tips
steps.body:
- Include collaboration and mentoring.
- Mention 1–2 growth areas honestly with what you're doing about them.
- Keep it concise: 3–5 key achievements.
- Keep a monthly 'brag doc' so you don't rely on memory.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing activities, not outcomes.
- Taking team credit as solely yours.
- Leaving it to the last hour before the deadline.

a.text: Your self-appraisal is due tomorrow. You have no notes. What do you do?

choices.label: Write generic lines quickly
Spend an hour pulling tickets, dashboards and emails to quantify 3–5 wins

b.text: Your manager asks for specifics during the review and you can't give them. What now?

choices.label: Send a follow-up with metrics within 2 days and start a monthly brag doc

c.text: You've written strong STAR points. Should you mention a weakness?

choices.label: Yes, one honest growth area with your action plan
No, claim you're perfect

d.text: Your manager uses your summary almost word-for-word in calibration.

e.text: Your manager raises gaps you ignored; your self-assessment seems less credible.

quiz.why: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Strong self-appraisal points include measurable results. Excuses and vague effort don't show impact.
A 'brag doc' is a running log of your achievements, a memory aid for appraisals.
Mentioning a growth area shows self-awareness and adds credibility.

quiz.q: How many key achievements to highlight?
quiz.why: Highlight 3 to 5 key achievements, for focus.

scenes.text: For two years Tarun hears 'not ready yet' without specifics.
He asks for the promotion criteria in writing and builds a plan.

steps.title: How promotions usually work
steps.body: Most companies have **level expectations** (scope, impact, leadership). Promotion cases are written by your manager, reviewed in a committee/calibration, and need **evidence that you're already working at the next level**, plus **sponsors** who speak for you.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body: 1) Ask for the next-level criteria. 2) Gap analysis with your manager. 3) Agree 2–3 stretch goals that show next-level work. 4) Gather evidence monthly. 5) Build visibility with senior leaders. 6) Ask: 'If I achieve these by March, will you put my case forward?'

steps.title: Solved example: gap plan
steps.body:
Next level (Senior Engineer) needs: owns a system end-to-end; mentors juniors; influences design across teams.
Tarun's gaps: mentoring and cross-team influence.
Plan: mentor 2 juniors; lead a cross-team design review; write a design doc adopted by two teams.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Asking 'Why not me?' without criteria.
- Comparing yourself to a colleague's promotion publicly.
- Threatening to quit as the first move.

a.text: You've been told 'not ready yet' twice. What do you do?

choices.label: Complain to peers that it's unfair
Ask for written next-level criteria and a gap plan

b.text: Your manager hears you're unhappy, but nothing changes. What now?

choices.label: Have a direct conversation about criteria

c.text: You agree three stretch goals. Six months later you've met them. What do you ask?

choices.label: 'I've met the agreed goals — will you put my case forward this cycle?'
'Promote me or I'll quit.'

d.text: Your manager submits your case with evidence; your sponsor supports it. You're promoted.

e.text: Your manager feels cornered. Even if you're promoted, trust is damaged. Lesson: evidence, not ultimatums.

quiz.q: Promotions usually require evidence that you:
options: Already work at the next level
quiz.why: Promotions usually require evidence that you already work at the next level.
After 'not ready yet', first ask for the criteria so you know what to work on.

quiz.q: An ultimatum ('promote me or I quit'):
quiz.why: An ultimatum like 'promote me or I quit' corners your manager and damages trust.

quiz.q: Who writes and defends your case?
quiz.why: Your manager writes and defends your promotion case, with sponsors. It isn't done by you alone.
Gap analysis compares your work with next-level criteria, giving you a plan.

lessons.title: Responding to an unfair rating or low hike

scenes.text: Zara gets a 'meets expectations' and a 4% hike after delivering a major launch.
She wants to react — but waits a day and plans.

steps.title: Pause first
steps.body: Don't reply in anger. Sleep on it. Then request a meeting: 'I'd like to understand the rating and what I can do differently.'

steps.title: In the conversation
steps.body:
- Ask for the reasons and examples.
- Share your evidence calmly (impact summary).
- Ask what would have earned the higher rating.
- Agree goals for next cycle and mid-year check-ins.
- If you believe the process was unfair (bias, missed evidence), use the formal **review/appeal** process with HR, factually.

steps.title: Solved example: the hike
steps.body: Market check: similar roles pay ~20% more. Zara asks: 'Given my scope and market data, can we discuss a correction or a mid-year review?' If not possible, she plans her options calmly — internal move or external search — without burning bridges.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Angry emails to leadership.
- Disengaging for months ('quiet quitting'), which confirms the rating.
- Comparing others' ratings publicly (ratings are confidential).

a.text: You receive a lower rating than you expected. It's 6 pm. What do you do?

choices.label: Email the VP tonight explaining why it's unfair
Sleep on it and request a meeting with your manager

b.text: The VP forwards your email to your manager. Now the relationship is tense. What now?

choices.label: Apologise for skipping your manager and request a calm discussion

c.text: Your manager explains that calibration rated the launch as 'team impact', not yours. You have evidence of your leadership. What do you do?

choices.label: Share your evidence, ask what would change the outcome, and use the formal review process if needed
Stop putting in effort

d.text: Your manager agrees to add evidence for a mid-year review and to sponsor you more strongly next cycle.

e.text: Your next rating drops further. Lesson: respond with evidence, not disengagement.

quiz.q: First reaction to a disappointing rating:
quiz.why: After a disappointing rating, pause before responding, to keep composure.

options: What would have earned a higher rating
quiz.why: In the discussion, ask what would have earned a higher rating, so you learn.
A formal appeal should be factual and go through the proper process.
Disengaging after a low rating usually confirms it in others' eyes.
Others' ratings are confidential, so don't ask about or share them.

questions.q: Bell-curve ratings are:
questions.why: Bell-curve ratings are relative, comparing people within a pool.

questions.q: STAR's R stands for:
questions.why: In STAR, R stands for Result.

questions.q: After a disappointing rating, first:
questions.why: After a disappointing rating, first pause. Reacting angrily or resigning immediately rarely helps.

questions.q: Promotion evidence shows:
questions.why: Promotion evidence shows you already do next-level work, not just long hours or seniority.

questions.q: Calibration is done by:
questions.why: Calibration is done by managers together.

questions.q: A brag doc helps:
questions.why: A brag doc helps you remember your achievements.

questions.q: Pool of 40, 15% top → top ratings:
questions.why: 15% of a pool of 40 is 0.15 × 40 = 6 top ratings.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Hard work alone guarantees a top rating. Reason (R): In forced distributions, ratings are relative and evidence-driven.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: in forced distributions ratings are relative and evidence-driven, so hard work alone doesn't guarantee a top rating.

questions.q: Best self-appraisal line:
options: 'Cut load time from 6 s to 2 s, raising conversions 8%'
questions.why: 'Cut load time from 6 s to 2 s, raising conversions 8%' is measurable. 'Worked hard' and 'did many tasks' don't show impact.

questions.q: Ultimatums for promotion:
questions.why: Ultimatums for promotion damage trust, because they corner your manager.

questions.q: Case: You believe a rating was biased and your manager won't discuss it. Step?
options: Use the formal HR review/appeal with evidence
questions.why: If you believe a rating was biased and your manager won't discuss it, use the formal HR review or appeal with evidence.

questions.q: Case: Two months before appraisal; leaders outside your team don't know your work. Best?
options: Present your project in a cross-team review
questions.why: Present your project in a cross-team review to gain visibility with leaders who don't know your work.

questions.q: Case: Low hike vs market. Constructive ask?
options: Discuss correction or mid-year review with market data
questions.why: For a low hike versus market, discuss a correction or mid-year review with market data. Threats or silent disengagement don't help.

questions.q: Why does your manager need a one-page impact summary before calibration?
options: To argue for you with specifics against other managers' evidence
questions.why: Your manager needs a one-page impact summary to argue for you with specifics against other managers' evidence in calibration.

questions.q: Which is the BEST promotion conversation opener?
options: 'What does the next level require, and what gaps do you see for me?'
questions.why: 'What does the next level require, and what gaps do you see for me?' is criteria-focused and collaborative. Comparisons or demands aren't.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Boundaries and ethics: when politics crosses a line
courses.summary: Telling tough politics from bullying, harassment and discrimination; refusing unethical requests; after-hours and drinking-culture pressure; and comments about caste, religion, region or gender.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish normal politics from misconduct
Learners can refuse unethical requests safely and document them
Learners can set boundaries on after-hours work and social pressure
Learners can respond to discriminatory comments as target or bystander

scenes.text: Nikhil's lead shouts at him in front of the team weekly and calls him 'useless'. Others say, 'That's just how he is.'
Nikhil learns that this has crossed from tough management into bullying.

steps.title: Where the line is
steps.body:
- **Normal politics:** competing priorities, persuasion, alliances, disagreements, tough-but-fair feedback.
- **Misconduct:** bullying (repeated humiliation, threats, shouting, exclusion), **sexual harassment** (covered by the POSH Act, 2013), **discrimination** (caste, religion, gender, disability, region, age), retaliation, fraud or ethics violations.
Misconduct should be reported through company channels, not 'managed politically'.

steps.title: If it's misconduct
steps.body: 1) Note dates, words, witnesses, evidence (messages). 2) If safe, ask clearly for it to stop. 3) Report to your manager (if not involved), HR, the ethics hotline, or the **Internal Committee** for sexual harassment. 4) Look after your health; use EAP or Tele-MANAS **14416** if stressed.

steps.title: Solved example: classify
steps.body:
- Lead rejects your proposal with reasons → normal politics.
- Lead calls you 'useless' in public every week → bullying.
- Colleague makes sexual jokes about you → sexual harassment (POSH).
- You're excluded from client meetings 'because of your community' → discrimination.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Normalising abuse as 'culture'.
- Waiting until you're burnt out to act.
- Retaliating instead of reporting.

activity.prompt: Normal politics or misconduct to report?

items.text: A peer lobbies leadership for their project over yours
Manager publicly humiliates you every week
Sexual comments about a colleague in a meeting
Being denied a role because of your religion
Your rating falls right after you reported fraud

quiz.q: Sexual harassment at work in India is addressed by:
options: The POSH Act, 2013 and the Internal Committee
quiz.why: Sexual harassment at work in India is addressed by the POSH Act, 2013 and the Internal Committee.
Repeated public humiliation is bullying, which is misconduct, not feedback or politics.

quiz.q: First practical step if facing misconduct:
quiz.why: If facing misconduct, first note dates, words and witnesses. This builds evidence.
Tele-MANAS, the mental health helpline, is 14416.

quiz.q: A rating cut after reporting fraud may be:
quiz.why: A rating cut after reporting fraud may be retaliation for the report, which is not allowed.

scenes.text: At quarter-end, Sameer's boss asks him to 'adjust' utilisation numbers so the client invoice is higher.
He's scared of losing his job — and of doing something wrong.

steps.title: How to say no
steps.body:
- Ask clarifying questions: 'Do you mean bill hours we didn't work?'
- Say no to the act, not the person: 'I'm not comfortable changing the data — can we show the real numbers and explain the variance?'
- Offer an ethical alternative.
- Put a neutral recap in writing.
- Escalate through the ethics hotline/compliance if pressured.

steps.title: Why refusing protects you
steps.body: 'My boss told me to' is not a defence for falsifying records, bribery or fraud. Speaking up in good faith is protected by most Codes of Conduct and, for listed companies, by vigil mechanisms.

steps.title: Solved example: recap email
steps.body: 'Hi Arun, following our call: I'll send the client the actual utilisation (82%) with a note on the two holiday weeks. Let me know if you'd like to discuss. — Sameer'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Agreeing 'just this once'.
- Confronting aggressively.
- Keeping no record.

a.text: Your manager asks you to inflate hours on a client invoice. What do you do?

choices.label: Do it — it's their responsibility
Decline politely, offer an honest alternative, and send a neutral recap

b.text: An audit flags the invoice. Your name is on it. What now?

choices.label: Cooperate fully and tell the truth
choices.feedback: Honesty is the best remaining option.

c.text: Your manager says, 'Team players do this. Think about your rating.' What next?

choices.label: Report through the ethics hotline/compliance
Give in

d.text: You face disciplinary action but your cooperation counts. Lesson: refuse at the start.

e.text: Compliance investigates; the threat is treated as retaliation risk. You're protected and the invoice is corrected.

quiz.why: 'My boss told me to' is not a defence for fraud, since you are personally responsible for your actions.

options: No to the act, offer an ethical alternative
quiz.why: The best way to refuse is to say no to the act and offer an ethical alternative. That is constructive.

quiz.q: A neutral recap email helps by:
quiz.why: A neutral recap email helps by documenting what was agreed.
A rating threat after refusing should be escalated, since it is a retaliation risk.
Agreeing 'just once' starts a slippery slope, as each step makes the next easier.

story.title: The 11 pm call and the team party

scenes.text: Lakshmi's manager calls at 11 pm 'just to discuss tomorrow'. It's becoming routine.
At team parties, colleagues push her to drink, though she doesn't.

steps.title: After-hours boundaries
steps.body:
- Distinguish true emergencies from habit.
- Propose norms: 'Unless it's urgent, could we cover these in the 9:30 call?'
- Use status and do-not-disturb settings; reply next morning to non-urgent messages.
- Be flexible for genuine crises, global time zones and launches — and ask for time back after.

steps.title: Social pressure
steps.body: You never have to drink, eat something against your beliefs, or stay late at parties. Simple lines: 'I'm good with my juice, thanks!' 'I'll head out early — great evening!' Good teams plan inclusive events (lunches, games) too.

steps.title: Solved example: proposing a norm
steps.body: 'I want to be responsive when it matters. For non-urgent things, could we use the morning call or a message I'll reply to by 9:30? For emergencies, please call anytime.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Never saying anything, then burning out.
- Lecturing others about their choices.
- Feeling you must explain personal or religious reasons — a polite 'no thanks' is enough.

a.text: Your manager calls you most nights after 10 pm about non-urgent things. What do you do?

choices.label: Keep answering and stay silent
Propose a norm for non-urgent topics and keep emergencies open

b.text: Months later you're exhausted and your work suffers. What now?

choices.label: Have the norm conversation and look after your health

c.text: At a team party, a senior insists you drink 'to be part of the team'. What do you do?

choices.label: Smile and say 'I'm good with my juice, thanks!'
Drink to avoid awkwardness

d.text: The senior moves on. Your manager agrees to the call norm. Boundaries respected.

e.text: You feel uncomfortable and the pressure repeats at every party. Lesson: a friendly, firm no works.

options: Non-urgent topics wait for working hours; emergencies anytime
quiz.why: A healthy after-hours norm is that non-urgent topics wait for working hours, while emergencies can come anytime.

quiz.q: You must drink at team events:
quiz.why: Drinking at team events is never required. It is a personal choice.
'I'm good with my juice, thanks!' is a simple, polite refusal.

options: Help and ask for time back later
quiz.why: For genuine crises you can help and ask for time back later, which keeps flexibility.

quiz.q: Explaining religious reasons for not drinking is:
quiz.why: Explaining religious reasons for not drinking is optional; 'no thanks' is enough.

lessons.title: Caste, religion, region and gender comments

scenes.text: At lunch, a colleague says to Arvind, 'You people from that state are always lazy.' Others laugh.
Another day, someone asks a new colleague her caste 'just casually'.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Stereotypes and questions about caste, religion, region, gender, skin colour or disability exclude people and can amount to **discrimination or harassment** under company policy and, in some cases, law (for example, India's laws protecting Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and disability rights law). 'Just joking' doesn't change the impact.

steps.title: If you're the target
steps.body:
- Short, calm response: 'That's a stereotype, and it's not okay.'
- Don't answer intrusive questions: 'I'd rather not discuss that at work.'
- Note details and report if repeated or serious.

steps.title: If you're a bystander
steps.body:
- **Interrupt:** 'Let's not go there.'
- **Support** the person privately.
- **Report** patterns.
Silence can feel like agreement to the person targeted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Positive' stereotypes ('your community is so good with money') — still stereotyping.
- Asking surnames to guess caste.
- Laughing along to avoid awkwardness.

This is general education, not legal advice.

a.text: A colleague makes a regional stereotype joke at lunch. People laugh. The person targeted looks uncomfortable. What do you do?

choices.label: Laugh along
Say lightly but clearly, 'Let's not go there,' and change topic

b.text: The targeted colleague stops joining lunches. What now?

choices.label: Apologise privately and speak up next time

c.text: Later, you check in with the colleague. They say it happens often. What do you do?

choices.label: Offer support and, with their consent, help them report the pattern
Report it publicly on the team channel without asking them
choices.feedback: Takes away their choice and exposes them.

d.text: HR addresses the pattern; the team gets inclusion training. Your colleague feels supported.

e.text: Your colleague feels exposed. Lesson: support, then act with consent.

quiz.q: Stereotype jokes about a region are:
quiz.why: Stereotype jokes about a region are exclusionary and may breach policy, whatever the intent.

quiz.q: Asking a colleague's caste at work is:
quiz.why: Asking a colleague's caste at work is intrusive and inappropriate, with privacy and discrimination risks.
'Positive' stereotypes are still stereotyping, because they generalise about a group.

quiz.q: As a bystander, a simple interruption is:
quiz.why: A simple bystander interruption is 'Let's not go there.' It defuses the situation.

quiz.q: Reporting on behalf of someone should be:
quiz.why: Reporting on someone's behalf should be done with their consent where possible, out of respect.

questions.q: Repeated public humiliation is:
questions.why: Repeated public humiliation is bullying, which is misconduct.

questions.q: Sexual harassment complaints go to:
questions.why: Sexual harassment complaints go to the Internal Committee under the POSH Act.

questions.q: You must drink at office parties:
questions.why: You never have to drink at office parties. It is your choice.

questions.q: Refusing an unethical request: say no to:
questions.why: Say no to the act, offering an alternative, not to the person angrily.

questions.q: Asking caste at work is:
questions.why: Asking caste at work is inappropriate, with discrimination risk.

questions.q: After-hours norm for non-urgent topics:
questions.why: Non-urgent topics should wait for working hours, as a boundary.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 'Just joking' makes stereotypes acceptable. Reason (R): Impact matters more than intent.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: impact matters more than intent, so 'just joking' doesn't make stereotypes acceptable.

questions.q: A rating threat after refusing fraud is:
questions.why: A rating threat after refusing fraud is a retaliation risk, so escalate it.

questions.q: Lobbying for your project is:
questions.why: Lobbying for your project is normal, legitimate politics, not fraud or harassment.

questions.q: Bystander support should be:
options: With the target's consent for reporting
questions.why: Bystander support should respect the target's consent for reporting, which preserves their agency.

questions.q: Case: Manager asks you to backdate a contract. Best response?
options: Decline, offer correct-date alternative, recap in writing, escalate if pressured
questions.why: Decline to backdate the contract, offer a correct-date alternative, recap in writing and escalate if pressured. Complying is fraud and shouting doesn't help.

questions.q: Case: You're asked 'What's your surname? Which community?' by a new colleague. Response?
options: 'I'd rather not discuss that at work.'
questions.why: 'I'd rather not discuss that at work' sets a polite boundary. You don't have to share your surname's community.

questions.q: Case: Lead shouts and calls people 'useless'; team says 'that's culture'. Best step?
options: Document incidents and report to HR/skip-level
questions.why: Document incidents and report to HR or a skip-level. 'That's culture' doesn't make shouting and insults acceptable.

questions.q: Why is documenting incidents important?
options: Patterns and facts are needed for fair investigation
questions.why: Documenting incidents matters because patterns and facts are needed for a fair investigation.

questions.q: Which BEST separates politics from misconduct?
options: Misconduct violates law/policy or dignity (bullying, harassment, discrimination, fraud); politics is legitimate influence
questions.why: Misconduct violates law, policy or dignity, as in bullying, harassment, discrimination and fraud. Politics is legitimate influence, so they are different.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Moving on: transfers, resignations and reputation
courses.summary: Asking for an internal transfer, resigning gracefully, handling counter-offers, notice periods and buyouts, relieving letters and background verification, and protecting your reputation.
outcomes: Learners can approach an internal transfer without burning bridges
Learners can resign professionally and handle a counter-offer
Learners understand notice periods, buyouts, relieving letters and BGV
Learners can leave with their reputation and network intact

scenes.text: Pooja wants to move to the data science team. She's afraid her manager will see it as betrayal.
She plans the conversation carefully.

steps.title: How to approach it
steps.body: 1) Check the internal mobility policy (minimum tenure, rating rules). 2) Tell your manager **before** applying, framed around growth, not escape. 3) Talk informally to the other team. 4) Offer a clean handover plan.

steps.title: Solved example: the conversation
steps.body: 'I've really learned a lot here. Long-term I want to grow in data science, and there's an opening in Ravi's team. I'd like to apply, and I'll make sure the handover is smooth — I could train Ajay over the next month. Would you support me?'

steps.title: If your manager resists
steps.body: Listen to concerns (timing, project risk), agree a realistic transition date, and involve HR if policy allows the move. Avoid going around your manager.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Your manager hearing about it from the other team first.
- Disengaging after applying.
- Criticising your current team to the new one.

a.text: You want to move to another team. What's your first step?

choices.label: Apply secretly and tell your manager only if selected
Check policy and tell your manager first, framed as growth

b.text: The other manager calls your manager for a reference. Your manager is upset. What now?

choices.label: Apologise, explain your goals, and propose a handover plan

c.text: Your manager worries about a deadline. What do you offer?

choices.label: A transition date after the deadline and a training plan for your replacement

d.text: Your manager supports the move and stays a supporter. You join the new team on good terms.

quiz.why: Before applying internally, tell your manager, for transparency.
Frame the move around growth, a positive reason. Escaping a bad boss or gossip looks negative.
A handover plan shows responsibility and professionalism.
First check the internal mobility policy for the rules.
After applying, keep performing well to protect your reputation.

scenes.text: Arjun has a signed offer. He's nervous about telling his manager.
His manager immediately offers a 25% raise to stay.

steps.title: How to resign
steps.body: 1) Have the new offer **in writing** first. 2) Tell your manager **in person or on a call** before emailing. 3) Be brief and positive: thank them, state your last day per notice. 4) Follow with a short formal email. 5) Don't announce publicly until your manager agrees on communication.

steps.title: Counter-offers
steps.body: Ask yourself: Why did I start looking? Will money fix that (role, manager, growth, culture)? Will trust be the same after? Accepting can work if the real issue is solved — but if the reasons were non-financial, they often return.

steps.title: Solved example: resignation email
steps.body: 'Dear Meera, as discussed today, I am resigning from my role as Senior Analyst. As per my 60-day notice period, my last working day will be 20 March. I'm grateful for the opportunities here and will ensure a smooth handover. Regards, Arjun'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Resigning by email without a conversation.
- Using a fake offer to get a raise — damages trust if discovered.
- Accepting an offer and then backing out at the last minute (it burns bridges with the new employer).

a.text: You resign; your manager offers a 25% raise. You left because of no growth and a difficult skip-level. What do you do?

choices.label: Accept immediately for the money
choices.feedback: Money doesn't fix growth or the skip-level.

choices.label: Thank them, reflect on whether the real issues would change, then decide

b.text: Six months later, nothing else has changed and you're unhappy again. What now?

choices.label: Learn the lesson and plan your next move carefully

c.text: You conclude the issues won't change. How do you decline?

choices.label: 'Thank you, I appreciate it. I've decided to take this step for my growth.'
Tell them everything wrong with the company

d.text: You leave on good terms; your manager becomes a reference.

e.text: Word spreads and your reputation suffers. Lesson: leave gracefully.

quiz.why: Before resigning, ensure you have a written offer. A verbal promise or rumour isn't safe.
Tell your manager in person or by call before emailing, out of respect.

options: The real reason for leaving is fixed
quiz.why: Counter-offers work best when the real reason for leaving is fixed. Money alone rarely solves it.

quiz.q: Backing out of a signed offer last minute:
quiz.why: Backing out of a signed offer at the last minute burns bridges.
Resignation emails should be brief and positive, not long complaints.

lessons.title: Notice period, buyout, relieving letter and BGV

scenes.text: Divya's contract has a 90-day notice; her new employer wants her in 30.
She learns the options: buyout, leave adjustment, negotiation — and why her relieving letter matters.

steps.title: Notice period and buyout
steps.body: Your **employment contract** sets the notice period (often 30–90 days in Indian tech). Options to leave earlier, depending on policy: the employer **waives** part of it, you **buy out** the remaining notice (pay basic or gross for the shortfall, as per contract), or adjust earned leave if allowed. Some new employers reimburse buyouts. Always check your contract and get agreements in writing.

steps.title: Documents to collect
steps.body:
- **Relieving letter** (confirms you were relieved of duties)
- **Experience/service letter**
- **Full and final (F&F) settlement** statement: last salary, leave encashment, bonus, deductions
- **Form 16** for the year
- **PF**: keep UAN; transfer to new employer

steps.title: Background verification (BGV)
steps.body: New employers often run BGV through agencies: previous employment dates, designation, sometimes reasons for leaving, education, address and references. Inconsistent dates, fake documents or 'absconding' (leaving without notice) can cost you the new job.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving without serving or settling notice ('absconding').
- Not collecting relieving letter and F&F.
- Inflating designation or dates on your CV — BGV checks them.

activity.prompt: Exit checklist
items: Read notice-period clause in my contract
Agreed last working day in writing
Returned laptop, ID card and assets

quiz.q: Notice period length is set by:
quiz.why: Notice period length is set by your employment contract or policy.

options: Paying for the unserved notice period
quiz.why: A buyout means paying for the unserved part of the notice period.
A relieving letter confirms you were relieved of your duties.
Background verification (BGV) commonly checks employment dates and designation.

options: Hurt your BGV and new job
quiz.why: Absconding can hurt your BGV and your new job.

scenes.text: On his last day, Kunal sends a warm farewell email with his LinkedIn and thanks to specific people.
Three years later, his old manager — now a director elsewhere — hires him.

steps.title: Leave well
steps.body:
- Finish or hand over cleanly; document everything.
- Thank people specifically.
- In exit interviews, be honest but constructive.
- Don't take confidential data.
- Keep in touch — many people return ('boomerang' hires) or meet old colleagues as clients.

steps.title: Solved example: farewell note
steps.body: 'Today is my last day. Thank you to Meera for trusting me with the payments launch, to Ravi for patient code reviews, and to the whole team for the laughs. I'd love to stay in touch: [LinkedIn]. All the best!'

steps.title: Reputation travels
steps.body: In India's industries, references are informal and fast — your last 3 months are remembered as much as your first 3 years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Coasting' in the notice period.
- Venting in the farewell email.
- Recruiting colleagues aggressively against your contract terms.

a.text: It's your notice period. Your manager asks you to document your systems. You're tempted to coast. What do you do?

choices.label: Do the minimum — you're leaving anyway
choices.feedback: The last months shape your reputation.

choices.label: Write thorough handover docs and train your replacement

b.text: The team struggles after you leave; your manager later gives a lukewarm informal reference. What now?

choices.label: Reach out, apologise, and offer a quick call to clarify open items

c.text: On your last day, how do you say goodbye?

choices.label: Warm, specific thanks and your contact details

d.text: Years later, a former colleague recommends you for a dream role. Leaving well pays off.

options: Someone who returns to a former employer
quiz.why: A 'boomerang' hire is someone who returns to a former employer.
Your performance during the notice period shapes your reputation, because colleagues remember how you left.
Exit interviews should be honest but constructive, so feedback is useful and you leave on good terms. Anger or sarcasm doesn't help.
Taking confidential data when leaving is a breach of confidentiality duties.
A good farewell note includes specific thanks and your contact details, which build goodwill.

questions.q: Before applying for an internal transfer, tell:
questions.why: Before applying for an internal transfer, tell your manager, for transparency.

questions.q: Resign first:
options: In a conversation with your manager
questions.why: Resign first in a conversation with your manager, out of respect. Using a peer or social media is disrespectful.

questions.q: Relieving letter is issued by:
questions.why: The relieving letter is issued by your former employer, confirming you were relieved of duties.

questions.q: Notice buyout means:
questions.why: A notice buyout means paying for the unserved part of the notice period.

questions.q: BGV checks:
questions.why: Background verification (BGV) checks dates and designation of past employment.

questions.q: Using a fake offer to get a raise:
questions.why: Using a fake offer to get a raise can destroy trust if it is discovered.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Counter-offers fix non-financial reasons for leaving. Reason (R): Issues like growth and manager fit aren't solved by money alone.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: issues like growth and manager fit aren't solved by money alone, so counter-offers often don't fix non-financial reasons.

questions.q: Absconding usually leads to:
questions.why: Absconding usually leads to problems in BGV and references, as the old employer won't verify a clean exit.

questions.q: F&F settlement covers:
questions.why: The F&F (full and final) settlement covers final salary, leave encashment and deductions.

questions.q: During notice, coasting:
questions.why: Coasting during notice damages your reputation, because people remember the last impression.

questions.q: Case: Contract says 90 days; new employer wants 30. Best path?
options: Request early release/waiver; discuss buyout per contract; get it in writing
questions.why: Request early release or a waiver, discuss a buyout per the contract and get it in writing. Ignoring the contract or faking illness is unprofessional.

questions.q: Case: Manager hears about your internal application from the other team. Repair?
options: Apologise, explain goals, offer handover plan
questions.why: Apologise, explain your goals and offer a handover plan, which repairs trust. Denying it makes things worse.

questions.q: Case: Exit interview asks why you're leaving; real reason is a toxic skip-level. Best?
questions.why: Share factual, constructive feedback in the exit interview, so the issue can be addressed. Ranting or lying helps no one.

questions.q: Why does inflating designation on a CV hurt?
options: BGV can catch it, risking offer withdrawal
questions.why: Inflating a designation on a CV can be caught by BGV, risking offer withdrawal.

questions.q: Which sequence is best when resigning?
options: Written offer → conversation with manager → formal email → handover → collect letters
questions.why: Get a written offer first, then speak to your manager, send a formal email, do the handover and collect your letters. Announcing on LinkedIn first is disrespectful.

courses.title: Office politics · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Principles summary, a rapid-fire scenario drill and a full mock test across all chapters.
outcomes: Learners can recall the core principles of ethical influence
Learners can choose the best move in mixed scenarios
Learners can score 80%+ on the mock

scenes.text: Before retiring, a respected senior writes ten principles for freshers.
They fit on one page.

steps.title: Power and influence
steps.body: Map formal and informal power · pre-align stakeholders · mentors advise, sponsors advocate · give first; never flatter or gossip.

steps.title: Managers
steps.body: Learn their preferences · no surprises · earn autonomy from micromanagers · protect credit calmly with documentation and visibility · never badmouth old bosses.

steps.title: Peers and appraisals
steps.body: Inclusive language and lunches · assume chats are public · calm, additive corrections · evidence for undermining · ratings are relative — equip your manager · STAR self-appraisals · promotion = next-level evidence + sponsors · pause before reacting.

steps.title: Boundaries and exits
steps.body: Misconduct (bullying, harassment, discrimination, fraud) is reported, not 'managed' · refuse unethical requests with alternatives · set after-hours norms · polite no to social pressure · transfers: tell your manager first · resign in person · leave well.

cards.back: Mentor advises; sponsor advocates using influence
Stay calm; add facts; discuss privately; document
No to the act, offer alternative, recap in writing, escalate if pressured
Pause, ask for reasons, share evidence, use formal review if needed
Written offer → talk to manager → formal email → handover

quiz.why: A sponsor uses their influence to advocate for you. Mentors advise.
Gossip as a tactic backfires because it erodes trust.
Misconduct should be reported through the proper process, not managed politically or joked about.
Leaving well includes a thorough handover, which protects your reputation.

scenes.text: Choose the best move quickly.
Then read why.

steps.title: Dilemma 1
steps.body: Director nods at your idea but nothing happens → find who influences the decision; pre-align them.

steps.title: Dilemma 2
steps.body: Boss pings hourly → propose fixed summary times; earn autonomy.

steps.title: Dilemma 3
steps.body: Peer says 'I built this' → 'Yes, and I built the charts…'; agree joint presenting.

steps.title: Dilemma 4
steps.body: Asked to inflate hours → decline, honest alternative, recap email, escalate if pressured.

steps.title: Dilemma 5
steps.body: Counter-offer after resigning for growth reasons → reflect; money rarely fixes growth.

a.text: Mixed round: In a WhatsApp group, a layoff 'list' with names is shared. What do you do?

choices.label: Forward to friends who might be affected
choices.feedback: Spreads possibly false and confidential info.

choices.label: Don't forward; report the leak to HR; ask your manager for clarity privately

b.text: The list turns out to be fake and people panic. What now?

choices.label: Apologise, delete, and report the original message

c.text: Next: appraisal is in two months, and senior leaders don't know your work. What do you do?

choices.label: Share an impact summary with your manager and offer to present in a cross-team review
Wait and hope

d.text: You handled both like a pro: trustworthy and visible.

e.text: You get a middle rating despite strong work. Lesson: equip your advocate.

quiz.why: A fake layoff list should not be forwarded, and should be reported, as it may harm people and breach confidentiality.
Before appraisal, share evidence of your impact and gain visibility, so your manager can advocate for you.
For hourly pings, propose fixed summaries, which reduce the manager's anxiety.
Decline a request to inflate hours, offer an alternative and document it. Complying would be dishonest.

scenes.text: Take the mock in 25 minutes.
Review every explanation.

steps.title: Pick answers that are
steps.body: **Calm** (no public fights) · **Direct** (talk privately first) · **Evidence-based** (notes, data) · **Ethical** (never fraud, gossip or flattery) · **Relationship-preserving** (no burned bridges).

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Ethics, safety, harassment, discrimination or retaliation → formal channels immediately. Everyday friction → direct conversation first.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: You can be both kind and strategic. The best 'politicians' at work are the people others trust.

activity.prompt: Which situation from this course are you facing right now, and what is your next step?
activity.hint: e.g. 'My boss takes credit — I'll ask to present the next update.'

quiz.why: For everyday friction, start with a direct private conversation. Proportion matters; HR is for more serious problems.
Harassment should go to formal channels immediately. It is serious misconduct, not politics or a joke.
The best workplace 'politicians' are trusted people, who influence honestly.

questions.q: Informal power comes from:
questions.why: Informal power comes from expertise and relationships, not just title, salary or age.

questions.q: Sponsor =
questions.why: A sponsor is an advocate who uses their influence for you.

questions.q: Chats with colleagues:
questions.why: Assume chats with colleagues are public, since screenshots can be shared.

questions.q: First step on a low rating:
questions.why: After a low rating, first pause before reacting. Resigning or posting online in anger rarely helps.

questions.q: High power, high interest:
questions.why: High power with high interest stakeholders should be managed closely.

questions.q: Credit-stealing peer in demo:
questions.why: With a credit-stealing peer in a demo, use a calm, additive correction, such as 'Yes, and I built the charts'. Public accusation or walking out hurts you.

questions.q: Drinking at office events:
questions.why: Drinking at office events is optional, never required for promotion.

questions.q: Relieving letter:
options: Confirms you were relieved of duties
questions.why: A relieving letter confirms you were relieved of duties. It isn't a salary slip, PF form or offer.

questions.q: Pool of 20, 15% top → top ratings:
questions.why: 15% of a pool of 20 is 0.15 × 20 = 3 top ratings.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Calibration rewards visible, evidenced impact. Reason (R): Managers compare people across teams.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: managers compare people across teams in calibration, so visible, evidenced impact is rewarded.

questions.q: Micromanager → earn autonomy by:
questions.why: A micromanager relaxes when you give proactive, scheduled updates, which builds trust and earns autonomy. Silence or confrontation raises anxiety.

questions.q: Regional stereotype joke → bystander:
questions.why: As a bystander to a regional stereotype joke, say 'Let's not go there' and support the target. Laughing, filming or forwarding is harmful.

questions.q: Case: Manager threatens rating if you refuse to backdate invoices. Step?
questions.why: A manager threatening your rating if you refuse to backdate invoices is retaliation. Escalate to ethics or compliance; don't comply.

questions.q: Case: New boss after reorg. First move?
options: Request intro with a one-page brief
questions.why: With a new boss after a reorg, request an intro with a one-page brief. This is proactive and sets the tone.

questions.q: Case: Counter-offer of +30%, but you left due to a toxic manager who stays. Likely outcome if you accept?
questions.why: If you accept a counter-offer without fixing the toxic manager, the core problem remains, even with +30%.

questions.q: Case: You want to move teams; policy needs 12 months, you have 14. Best approach?
options: Tell your manager first, frame as growth, offer handover
Ask the other team to poach you
questions.why: You meet the 12-month policy, so tell your manager first, frame the move as growth and offer a handover. Applying secretly or threatening to quit damages trust.

questions.q: Which is unethical influence?
questions.why: Spreading rumours about a rival is unethical influence, a form of manipulation. Pre-aligning, helping others and presenting evidence are ethical.

questions.q: Which best handles a 90-day notice when the new job wants 30?
options: Ask for waiver/buyout per contract, in writing
questions.why: Ask for a waiver or buyout per the contract, in writing. Absconding, faking medical leave or ignoring emails harms your reputation and BGV.

questions.q: Why should skip-levels not become complaint sessions?
options: It damages trust with your manager; use them for work, ideas and serious issues only
questions.why: Skip-levels shouldn't become complaint sessions because it damages trust with your manager. Use them for work, ideas and serious issues.

questions.q: Which statement best summarises ethical office politics?
options: Understand how decisions are made and influence them honestly, while protecting dignity and integrity
questions.why: Ethical office politics means understanding how decisions are made and influencing them honestly while protecting dignity and integrity. It isn't flattery or winning at any cost.
